blocks.html: In the geologic time scale you met deep time: Earth is about 4.54 billion years old. This lesson asks two questions. How did a planet with layers, a metal core, a rocky mantle and a thin crust come to be? And how can we know its age so precisely when the planet keeps destroying its own oldest rocks?

About 4.6 billion years ago, a disk of gas and dust circled the young Sun. Dust grains stuck together into pebbles, pebbles into kilometer-sized planetesimals, and those crashed together into planets. Every collision turned motion into heat. Add the heat of short-lived radioactive elements, and the young Earth grew hot enough to melt in large part.

Melted rock and metal separate the way oil and water do: the denser liquid sinks. Iron and nickel (about 7 to 8 g/cm³ at the surface, more under pressure) drained toward the center, while lighter silicate rock (about 3 g/cm³) floated up. Geologists call this sorting by density differentiation. It left Earth layered: a metal core, a rocky mantle, and the lightest rock as a thin crust. A planet that never melted would be an even mix all the way through.

Earth formed about 4.54 billion years ago from colliding rock and metal. While it was hot, dense iron sank to make the core and lighter rock rose to make the mantle and crust. Its age comes from meteorites and Moon rocks, because Earth's own first crust has been recycled.

blocks.cap: Earth's layers by composition. Drag the probe down to see how density, pressure and temperature rise toward the center.

blocks.title: Why the inside must be dense
blocks.q: Earth's mass is $5.97 \times 10^{24}\,\text{kg}$ and its volume is $1.08 \times 10^{21}\,\text{m}^3$. Surface rocks average about $2.7$ to $3.0\,\text{g/cm}^3$. What does Earth's mean density tell us?
steps: Mean density: $\rho = \dfrac{m}{V} = \dfrac{5.97 \times 10^{24}}{1.08 \times 10^{21}} \approx 5,530\,\text{kg/m}^3$.
Divide by 1,000 to get g/cm³: about $5.5\,\text{g/cm}^3$.
That is about twice the density of surface rock. Rock squeezed by pressure gets a little denser, but not nearly enough: there must be something much denser deep inside, an iron core.
blocks.a: About $5.5\,\text{g/cm}^3$: far denser than surface rock, so Earth has a heavy metal core.

blocks.title: How long before the oldest rocks?
blocks.q: Earth formed about 4,540 million years ago. Its oldest known rocks, in northern Canada, are about 4,000 million years old, and its oldest known mineral grains (zircons from Australia) about 4,400 million years old. How much time passed before each?
steps: Before the oldest grains: $4,540 - 4,400 = 140$ million years.
Before the oldest rocks: $4,540 - 4,000 = 540$ million years.
For more than half a billion years, no rock survived intact. The early crust was melted by impacts, eroded and pulled back into the mantle.
blocks.a: About 140 million years before the oldest grains and 540 million years before the oldest rocks.

blocks.html: It is natural to think Earth's age must come from its oldest rocks. But those are only about 4.0 billion years old, because plate tectonics and erosion keep recycling crust; almost no ocean floor is older than about 200 million years. The 4.54-billion-year age comes from radiometric dates on meteorites, leftover pieces from when the planets formed, which agree with the oldest Moon rocks and the oldest Earth minerals. Check: if the oldest rocks gave Earth's age, no mineral grain could be older than them, yet zircons of 4.4 billion years exist.

blocks.cap: All of Earth's history squeezed into one year. Earth forms at the first moment of January 1; the oldest rocks appear in mid-February.

blocks.html: In Earthquakes and Seismic Waves you met the two body waves: fast P waves that push and pull, and slower S waves that shake side to side. No one has ever drilled through the crust; the deepest hole stops at about 12 km. Yet we have a detailed map of the inside, down to the center 6,371 km below us. Seismic waves drew it.

Two facts do the work. First, a wave bends (refracts) when its speed changes, just as light bends entering water. Rock gets stiffer with depth, so waves speed up and curve back toward the surface. Second, S waves are shear waves: they need the material to spring back when it is twisted. Solids do; liquids don't. So S waves cannot travel through a liquid, while P waves can, only more slowly.

items: The S-wave shadow. Beyond about $103^\circ$ around Earth from an earthquake, no direct S waves arrive. Something liquid and huge blocks them: the outer core.

The P-wave shadow. From about $103^\circ$ to $142^\circ$, no direct P waves arrive either. P waves slow sharply as they enter the outer core (from about 13.7 to 8 km/s), bend away and land beyond $142^\circ$.
The inner core. In 1936 Inge Lehmann noticed faint P waves inside the shadow zone. They had bounced off a solid inner core, where P waves speed up again.

blocks.name: es-interior
blocks.cap: P waves (blue) and S waves (red) leaving an earthquake at the top. Watch the S waves stop at the outer core, and the gap the P waves leave between about $103^\circ$ and $142^\circ$.

blocks.html: The layers were found by seismic waves, not drilling. S waves stop at a liquid outer core, leaving a shadow beyond $103^\circ$; P waves bend at the core and leave a shadow from about $103^\circ$ to $142^\circ$. The size of the shadows gives the size of the core.

blocks.title: Which station hears what?
blocks.q: Stations stand $60^\circ$, $125^\circ$ and $160^\circ$ around Earth from an earthquake. What does each record?
steps: $60^\circ$ is less than $103^\circ$: waves reach it through the solid mantle, so it records both P and S.
$125^\circ$ is between $103^\circ$ and $142^\circ$: in the P-wave shadow and beyond the S limit, so no direct P or S.
$160^\circ$ is beyond $142^\circ$: P waves arrive after crossing the core, but no S waves.
blocks.a: $60^\circ$: P and S. $125^\circ$: neither. $160^\circ$: P only.

blocks.title: How far is 103°?
blocks.q: Earth's radius is 6,371 km. How far along the surface is $103^\circ$ from an earthquake?
steps: Circumference: $2\pi r = 2\pi(6,371) \approx 40,030\,\text{km}$.
$103^\circ$ is $\tfrac{103}{360}$ of a full turn: $\tfrac{103}{360} \times 40,030 \approx 11,450\,\text{km}$.
Every large earthquake throws a shadow more than 11,000 km away, and stations worldwide see it each time.

blocks.html: Many people think the layers were found by drilling, or that lava comes up from the core. The deepest borehole, in Russia, reached about 12.3 km: just $0.2\%$ of the way to the center. Lava comes from partly melted rock in the upper mantle and crust. Check yourself: on a globe 20 cm across, the deepest hole would be about 0.4 mm deep.

blocks.html: Deep mines are hot. The deepest gold mines in South Africa reach about 4 km, where the rock is around 60 °C and the tunnels must be cooled. Temperature rising with depth, the geothermal gradient, is the first clue that Earth is a heat engine. In Half-Life and Absolute Age you met radioactive atoms; they are part of the story.

Heat flows from hot to cold. Earth's interior is hot for two reasons: leftover heat from the collisions and sinking iron that built the planet, and radioactive decay of uranium, thorium and potassium, which keeps adding heat. That heat must leak out through the crust. Rock conducts heat poorly, so a steady flow needs a steep temperature drop across it, the way a thick blanket keeps a big difference between your skin and the air. The rule for conduction is $q = k\,\dfrac{\Delta T}{\Delta z}$: heat flow $q$ equals the rock's conductivity $k$ times the gradient.

Temperature rises about $25^\circ\text{C}$ per km in the upper crust: $T = T_0 + g z$. The gradient is steep only near the surface. Deeper down, the mantle slowly convects and carries heat far better, so the temperature climbs gently, reaching about 5,000 to 6,000 °C at the center.

blocks.name: es-interior
blocks.cap: Estimated temperatures down to the center, against the straight line you would get by keeping the crust's gradient all the way down.

blocks.title: Temperature in a well
blocks.q: The surface is $15^\circ\text{C}$ and the gradient is $25^\circ\text{C/km}$. How hot is the rock at the bottom of a well 3 km deep?
steps: Warming: $25 \times 3 = 75^\circ\text{C}$.

blocks.title: Heat flow through the crust
blocks.q: Granite conducts heat with $k = 3.0\,\text{W/(m·K)}$. The gradient is $25^\circ\text{C/km}$. How much heat flows out through each square meter?
steps: Write the gradient in SI units: $25^\circ\text{C/km} = 0.025\,\text{K/m}$ (a change of 1 °C is a change of 1 K).
That is tiny next to sunlight (about $240\,\text{W/m}^2$ absorbed on average), but over all of Earth it adds up to roughly 45 terawatts, and it drives volcanoes, earthquakes and moving plates.

blocks.html: A common slip is to carry the crust's gradient all the way down: $15 + 25 \times 6,371 \approx 160,000^\circ\text{C}$ at the center, hotter than the Sun's surface. The real center is about 5,000 to 6,000 °C. The gradient is steep only where heat must squeeze through rock by conduction. Check any straight-line estimate against what the deep rock is doing: the mantle is solid but flows, and flowing rock carries heat.

blocks.html: In Lithosphere and Asthenosphere you learned that the rigid lithosphere rests on hot, slowly flowing asthenosphere. Over thousands of years that rock behaves like a very thick fluid, so the crust floats on it. Floating explains a surprising fact: the highest mountains have the deepest roots.

An object floats when it pushes aside its own weight of fluid (a formula we can solve for any letter): $\rho_{\text{object}} V_{\text{total}} = \rho_{\text{fluid}} V_{\text{under}}$. Ice ($0.917\,\text{g/cm}^3$) in seawater ($1.025$) floats about $89\%$ under. Crust ($2.7$) floats on mantle ($3.3$) the same way. Now compare two columns of the same width. Deep below both, at the bottom of the deepest root, the weight above each square meter must be the same; if it weren't, the soft mantle would flow until it was. A column with a mountain of height $h$ on top carries extra crust, so it must swap dense mantle for light crust below: a root $r$. Balancing the extra weight on top against the buoyancy gained below, $\rho_c h = (\rho_m - \rho_c)\,r$.

Crust floats on the mantle in isostatic balance. A range of height $h$ sits on a root $r = h\dfrac{\rho_c}{\rho_m - \rho_c}$. With crust $2.7$ and mantle $3.3\,\text{g/cm}^3$, $r = 4.5h$: most of a mountain range is underground.

blocks.name: es-density
blocks.cap: Crust floating on the mantle. Raise the mountain and watch the root grow 4.5 times as fast.

blocks.title: The root of a range
blocks.q: A range stands 4 km above the plains. Crust $2.7$, mantle $3.3\,\text{g/cm}^3$. How deep is its root?
steps: $r = 18\,\text{km}$. If normal crust there is 35 km thick, the crust under the peaks is $4 + 35 + 18 = 57\,\text{km}$ thick, close to what seismic waves find under the Andes.

blocks.title: Land pushed down by ice
blocks.q: An ice sheet 3 km thick ($\rho_{\text{ice}} = 0.917$) rests on the land for thousands of years. How far does the land sink into the mantle ($3.3$)?
steps: At balance, the ice's weight equals the weight of mantle pushed aside: $0.917 \times 3 = 3.3\,d$.
$d = \dfrac{2.751}{3.3} \approx 0.83\,\text{km}$.
When the ice melted at the end of the last ice age, the land began to rise back. Around Hudson Bay and the Baltic Sea it is still rising, up to about a centimeter a year.

blocks.html: It is tempting to picture mountains sitting on a flat base of solid rock that holds them up. If that were true, all that extra rock would tug hard on things nearby. In the 1850s, surveyors in India found that the Himalayas pull plumb lines sideways far less than their mass should: the extra rock above is balanced by light crust replacing dense mantle below. Check with the iceberg: you never see an iceberg standing tall on a flat bottom; the higher it rises, the deeper it reaches.

blocks.html: A compass works because Earth has a magnetic field, as if a giant bar magnet lay along its axis. Seismic waves showed the outer core is liquid iron. Here we see how that field is made, how rocks record it, and why the record turned out to be some of the strongest evidence for moving plates.

Iron loses its permanent magnetism when it is hot: above about $580^\circ\text{C}$ (the Curie temperature) magnetite can't hold a direction. The core is thousands of degrees hotter, so it cannot be a permanent magnet. Instead, liquid iron churns in the outer core. Moving electric conductors in a magnetic field make electric currents, and those currents make the field: a self-sustaining geodynamo. A dynamo can drift and even flip, and the record shows it does.

items: Recording. As lava cools through about $580^\circ\text{C}$, tiny magnetite grains line up with the field and freeze in place: a compass needle in stone.
Reversals. Lava flows of different ages point two opposite ways. The whole field has flipped many times at irregular intervals; the last flip was about 0.77 million years ago.

Inclination. Field lines are flat at the equator and point steeply down near the magnetic poles. For a dipole field, $\tan I = 2\tan\lambda$, so the dip $I$ frozen in a rock tells the latitude $\lambda$ where it formed (tangent again).

blocks.html: Earth's field is made by moving liquid iron in the outer core, not a solid magnet. Cooling lava records the field's direction and dip, so rocks keep a timeline of reversals and a record of the latitude where they formed.

blocks.name: es-boundary
blocks.cap: New seafloor records the field as it forms at a ridge. Normal (dark) and reversed (light) stripes build up symmetrically on both sides.

blocks.title: Latitude from a rock
blocks.q: Old lava records an inclination of $49^\circ$. At what latitude did it cool?
steps: $\tan\lambda = \dfrac{\tan 49^\circ}{2} = \dfrac{1.150}{2} = 0.575$.
$\lambda = \tan^{-1}(0.575) \approx 30^\circ$.
If the same rock now sits at $55^\circ$ N, its plate has carried it about $25^\circ$ north, roughly $25 \times 111 \approx 2,800\,\text{km}$.

blocks.title: How deep can rock stay magnetic?
blocks.q: With a surface temperature of $15^\circ\text{C}$ and a gradient of $25^\circ\text{C/km}$, how deep does the crust reach $580^\circ\text{C}$?
steps: Warming needed: $580 - 15 = 565^\circ\text{C}$.
Depth: $565 \div 25 \approx 23\,\text{km}$.
Below a few tens of kilometers, no rock can hold permanent magnetism, which is why the field must come from flowing metal.

blocks.html: Picturing a giant bar magnet of solid iron in the core is a natural guess, and the field's shape does look like one. But a hot magnet loses its magnetism, and a permanent magnet could not flip back and forth. Check: the core is above about $4,000^\circ\text{C}$, far past iron's Curie temperature of about $770^\circ\text{C}$.

blocks.html: In What Makes a Mineral you learned that a mineral is a natural solid with a definite chemistry and an orderly inner structure. In Ions you met atoms that have gained or lost electrons. Put the two together and you have the inside of most minerals: positive and negative ions stacked in a pattern that repeats in every direction.

Opposite charges attract. In halite (rock salt), each $\text{Na}^{+}$ is surrounded by six $\text{Cl}^{-}$ and each $\text{Cl}^{-}$ by six $\text{Na}^{+}$, a pattern that repeats trillions of times. Two rules shape every mineral. First, the crystal as a whole must be electrically neutral: positive charges cancel negative ones. Second, ions must fit the spaces in the pattern, which depends on their size. So any ion with the same charge and nearly the same size can take another's place without breaking either rule.

items: $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ (radius about 72 pm) and $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ (about 78 pm) trade places freely. That is why olivine ranges from $\text{Mg}_2\text{SiO}_4$ (forsterite) to $\text{Fe}_2\text{SiO}_4$ (fayalite), written $(\text{Mg},\text{Fe})_2\text{SiO}_4$.

$\text{Na}^{+}$ (102 pm) is the right size to replace $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ (100 pm) but carries the wrong charge. In plagioclase feldspar the swap still happens, paired with $\text{Al}^{3+}$ replacing $\text{Si}^{4+}$ to keep the balance: a coupled substitution.

blocks.html: A mineral is ions stacked in a repeating, electrically neutral pattern. Ions of similar size and the same charge can substitute for one another, so many minerals have a formula that varies within set limits.

blocks.name: es-minerals
blocks.cap: Olivine on the test bench. Its green color comes from iron; more iron makes it darker and denser.

blocks.title: Balance a formula
blocks.q: Garnet (pyrope) has 3 $\text{Mg}^{2+}$, 3 $\text{Si}^{4+}$ and 12 $\text{O}^{2-}$ per formula unit, plus some $\text{Al}^{3+}$. How many aluminum ions?
steps: Aluminum must bring $+6$: $6 \div 3 = 2$ ions.
The formula is $\text{Mg}_3\text{Al}_2\text{Si}_3\text{O}_{12}$.

blocks.title: A forsterite number
blocks.q: An olivine has 1.8 $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and 0.2 $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ per formula unit. What fraction of its metal sites hold magnesium?
steps: There are always 2 sites: $1.8 + 0.2 = 2$.
Magnesium fills $1.8 \div 2 = 0.90$ of them: geologists write Fo90.
Olivine near Fo90 is typical of Earth's upper mantle.

blocks.html: It is easy to think a mineral's formula is always exact, the way water is always $\text{H}_2\text{O}$. Many minerals are solid solutions: olivine can be any mix from all magnesium to all iron, and it is still olivine because the structure is the same. Check a substitution by asking two questions: is the charge the same (or balanced by a second swap), and is the size within about 15%?

blocks.html: Oxygen and silicon are the two most common elements in Earth's crust: by mass, about 47% oxygen and 28% silicon. In Atoms, Ions and Crystals you saw minerals as stacked ions. In the crust, the most important stack starts with one small building block.

A silicon ion, $\text{Si}^{4+}$, is tiny; an oxygen ion, $\text{O}^{2-}$, is large. The best way to pack them is four oxygens around each silicon, at the corners of a tetrahedron (a pyramid with four triangular faces). Its charge is $+4 + 4(-2) = -4$, so a lone tetrahedron is written $\text{SiO}_4^{4-}$. Something must cancel that $-4$. There are two ways: surround the tetrahedra with positive ions (such as $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and $\text{Fe}^{2+}$), or let neighboring tetrahedra share corner oxygens. A shared oxygen belongs half to each tetrahedron, so every shared corner raises the charge per silicon by 1.
The silica tetrahedron, one $\text{Si}^{4+}$ bonded to four $\text{O}^{2-}$, has charge $-4$. Positive ions or shared oxygens balance it. Count charge as $+4$ per silicon and $-2$ per oxygen.

blocks.name: es-minerals
blocks.cap: One tetrahedron, and a view from above of isolated tetrahedra with metal ions (green) between them, as in olivine. Switch the structure to see tetrahedra share corners.

blocks.title: How many magnesium ions?
blocks.q: How many $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ ions balance one $\text{SiO}_4^{4-}$ tetrahedron?
steps: The tetrahedron carries $-4$.
Each $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ brings $+2$: $4 \div 2 = 2$ ions.
That is forsterite, $\text{Mg}_2\text{SiO}_4$.

blocks.title: A ring of six
blocks.q: Six tetrahedra join in a closed ring, each sharing two corners with its neighbors. How many oxygens does the ring have, and what is its charge?
steps: Six separate tetrahedra would have $6 \times 4 = 24$ oxygens.
A ring of six has six links, and each link shares one oxygen: $24 - 6 = 18$. The group is $\text{Si}_6\text{O}_{18}$.
Charge: $6(+4) + 18(-2) = 24 - 36 = -12$. Beryl, the mineral behind emerald, is built of such rings.

blocks.html: A frequent slip is to get the tetrahedron's charge wrong: writing $-2$ (oxygen's charge alone) or $+4$ (silicon's). Add all five ions: $+4 - 8 = -4$. And remember that shared oxygens are counted once for the pair, which is why linked silicates carry less charge per silicon. Check: a fully shared framework, $\text{SiO}_2$ (quartz), comes out to $+4 - 4 = 0$, neutral, needing no other ions.

blocks.html: The silica tetrahedron can stand alone or share corners. How many corners each tetrahedron shares sorts nearly all the crust's minerals into five families, and that one structural fact explains their formulas, their shapes and the way they break.

mica, clay: one perfect cleavage into sheets
blocks.cap: The five silicate families.

blocks.html: Count oxygens per silicon: each unshared oxygen counts 1, each shared one counts $\tfrac12$. With $s$ shared corners, oxygens per silicon $= 4 - \tfrac{s}{2}$. Cleavage follows the weakest bonds. Inside a chain or sheet, Si–O bonds are strong; between chains or sheets, only weaker bonds through metal ions hold things together, so the crystal splits there. In quartz, every oxygen is shared in all three directions, leaving no weak plane at all, so it breaks along curved, shell-like surfaces.

Tetrahedra link as isolated units, single chains, double chains, sheets or frameworks. Oxygens per silicon $= 4 - \tfrac{s}{2}$ for $s$ shared corners, and cleavage runs between the strongly bonded chains or sheets.

blocks.name: es-minerals
blocks.cap: Tetrahedra linked into a sheet, seen from above; shared oxygens are marked. Switch structures and watch the silicon-to-oxygen ratio and the charge change.

blocks.title: From formula to family
blocks.q: Talc is $\text{Mg}_3\text{Si}_4\text{O}_{10}(\text{OH})_2$. Which family is it?
steps: Count the oxygens bonded to silicon (leave out the OH): $\text{Si}_4\text{O}_{10}$.
Ratio: $10 \div 4 = 2.5$ oxygens per silicon.
2.5 is the sheet ratio. Talc is a sheet silicate, which is why it is soft and slippery: the sheets slide past one another.

blocks.title: Why double chains give 2.75
blocks.q: In a double chain, half the tetrahedra share 2 corners and half share 3. How many oxygens per silicon?
steps: Average shared corners: $\tfrac{2 + 3}{2} = 2.5$.
Oxygens per silicon: $4 - \tfrac{2.5}{2} = 2.75$, so the repeat unit is $\text{Si}_4\text{O}_{11}$.

blocks.html: It is tempting to memorize the five family names without their structures, and then it seems arbitrary that mica peels into sheets while quartz has no cleavage. Tie each property to the linking: sheets peel, chains split along their length at angles set by their width, and a framework has no weak direction. Check yourself with feldspar: also a framework, but its aluminum and the large ions between tetrahedra leave two planes of weaker bonds, so it does cleave.

Silicates make up over 90% of the crust, but the rest include the minerals we mine most: metal ores, salt, limestone, gypsum. Like every mineral, each is built of positive and negative ions. Geologists sort them by their negative ion, because minerals that share one tend to share a structure and behave alike.

Examples

blocks.html: The negative ion sets a mineral's chemistry. Carbonates all fizz in acid, because $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ reacts with $\text{H}^{+}$ to release carbon dioxide gas. Sulfides form where there is little oxygen, often from hot fluids deep underground, and many are metal ores. Sulfates and halides crystallize as salty water evaporates. To write a formula, balance the charges: $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ and $\text{O}^{2-}$ need two irons for three oxygens, $\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3$.

Non-silicates are grouped by their negative ion: carbonates, oxides, sulfides, sulfates, halides and native elements. "-ide" means the bare element (sulfide, S); "-ate" means it comes with oxygen (sulfate, $\text{SO}_4$).

blocks.name: es-minerals
blocks.cap: Calcite on the test bench. Try the acid test: carbonates fizz.

blocks.title: Which group?
blocks.q: Barite is $\text{BaSO}_4$. Which group?
steps: Its negative ion is $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$: sulfur with oxygen.
So barite is a sulfate.

blocks.title: Write a formula
blocks.q: Fluorite is made of $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ and $\text{F}^{-}$ ions. Write its formula.
steps: One $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ brings $+2$; each $\text{F}^{-}$ brings $-1$.
Two fluorides balance one calcium: $\text{CaF}_2$.

blocks.html: Sulfides and sulfates are easy to mix up because their names differ by one syllable. Pyrite, $\text{FeS}_2$, is a sulfide: sulfur and no oxygen, a shiny brassy ore mineral. Gypsum, $\text{CaSO}_4 \cdot 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$, is a sulfate: each sulfur carries four oxygens, and it is soft enough to scratch with a fingernail. Check the formula for an O after the S.

blocks.html: The geothermal gradient told us the mantle is hot, over $1,300^\circ\text{C}$ at 100 km. Yet the mantle is almost entirely solid: the S waves that cross it prove that. So magma must form only in special places, where something tips solid rock past its melting point. Plate boundaries are exactly those places.

A rock melts when its temperature rises above its melting point (the solidus). There are three ways to get there, and only one involves adding heat. Pressure squeezes atoms together and makes melting harder, so the melting point of mantle rock rises steeply with depth. Water breaks bonds in the rock's minerals and lowers the melting point by hundreds of degrees.

items: Decompression melting (mid-ocean ridges, hot spots, rifts): hot mantle rises and keeps nearly all its heat, but the pressure drops, so its melting point falls below its temperature.
Flux melting (subduction zones): the sinking plate releases water into the hot mantle above it, lowering that rock's melting point.
Heat transfer: hot basalt magma rising into the crust can melt the crust around it, which melts at lower temperatures than the mantle.

blocks.html: Most magma forms without extra heat: rising rock melts because the pressure drops, and wet rock melts because water lowers the melting point. Hot magma can also melt the crust it rises into.

blocks.name: es-interior
blocks.cap: Temperature against depth. Follow the rising rock (the path) as it crosses the dry melting curve. The wet curve sits hundreds of degrees lower.

blocks.title: Where rising mantle starts to melt
blocks.q: Under a ridge, rising rock at depth $z$ km is about $T = 1,350 + 0.4z$ °C, and its melting point is about $T_m = 1,120 + 4z$ °C. At what depth does it start to melt?
steps: Set them equal: $1,350 + 0.4z = 1,120 + 4z$.
$230 = 3.6z$, so $z \approx 64\,\text{km}$.
Above 64 km, the rock is hotter than its melting point and a few percent of it melts. That melt rises and builds new ocean crust.

blocks.title: Wet or dry?
blocks.q: At 100 km, mantle rock is at $1,100^\circ\text{C}$. Dry rock there melts at about $1,300^\circ\text{C}$; with water, about $850^\circ\text{C}$. What happens above a sinking slab?
steps: Dry: $1,100 < 1,300$, so the rock stays solid.
With water from the slab: $1,100 > 850$, so it partly melts.
That is how the Andes and the Cascades get their magma.
blocks.a: It melts only where the slab supplies water.

blocks.html: It is natural to think magma forms by heating rock up. Under ridges and hot spots, though, rock melts as it rises and the pressure drops; at subduction zones, it melts because water is added. Check yourself: under a mid-ocean ridge nothing is heating the mantle, yet it produces about 20 cubic kilometers of new crust every year.

blocks.html: Melted rock is a mixture of many elements, not a pure liquid like water. In the early 1900s Norman Bowen melted rock powders in a laboratory furnace, cooled them step by step, and looked at which minerals grew at each temperature. His result, now called Bowen's reaction series, links the silicate families to the way magma freezes.

A mixture freezes over a range of temperatures, not at one point. As magma cools, the minerals with the strongest structures, built from iron, magnesium and silica-poor recipes, become stable first and crystallize. Each crystal takes its ingredients out of the melt, so the liquid left behind keeps changing: poorer in iron, magnesium and calcium, richer in silica, sodium and potassium. Minerals at the cool end form from that leftover melt.

blocks.html: As magma cools, minerals crystallize in order: olivine and calcium-rich plagioclase first, then pyroxene, amphibole and biotite, and potassium feldspar, muscovite and quartz last. The leftover melt grows richer in silica.

blocks.title: First to crystallize
blocks.q: Which crystallizes first from a cooling magma: amphibole, quartz, olivine or biotite?
steps: Olivine sits at the hot top of the series.
Order: olivine, amphibole, biotite, quartz.

blocks.title: The melt left behind
blocks.q: A magma is 50% silica. 40% of it crystallizes as olivine and calcium-rich plagioclase averaging 44% silica, and the crystals sink away. What percent silica is the remaining melt?
steps: Take 100 g of magma: 50 g of silica.
The 40 g of crystals hold $40 \times 0.44 = 17.6\,\text{g}$ of silica.
Left: $50 - 17.6 = 32.4\,\text{g}$ of silica in $60\,\text{g}$ of melt: $32.4 \div 60 = 54\%$.
Removing silica-poor crystals drives the melt toward andesite and, eventually, rhyolite composition.

blocks.html: Many people picture a magma freezing all at once, like a pond turning to ice. In fact different minerals form over several hundred degrees of cooling, and crystals can grow while plenty of liquid remains. Check with a real rock: in a slowly cooled granite, quartz fills the odd-shaped spaces between earlier feldspar and mica crystals, because it was the last to grow.

Bowen's series showed that melts range from silica-poor to silica-rich. Geologists name magmas, and the rocks they make, by that one number: the percent of silica ($\text{SiO}_2$) by mass. Silica controls how hot a magma is, how dark its rock will be, and above all how sticky it is.

blocks.cap: "Mafic" comes from magnesium and ferrum (iron); "felsic" from feldspar and silica.

blocks.html: Silica tetrahedra don't wait for the magma to freeze before linking up: even in the melt they share oxygens and form chains and networks. The more silica, the more links, and the harder the liquid is to stir. Felsic magma can be millions of times more viscous than basalt. Felsic magma is also cooler, because the minerals it makes sit at the cool end of Bowen's series, and cooler liquids are stickier still.
Magmas run from mafic (low silica, hot, runny, dark rock) to felsic (high silica, cooler, sticky, light rock). Silica links into networks in the melt, so more silica means much higher viscosity.

blocks.name: es-igneous
blocks.cap: Slide the silica content from 45% to 75% and watch the class, temperature, color and stickiness change.

blocks.title: Classify a magma
blocks.q: A magma is 58% silica. How is it classified?
steps: 58% is between 52% and 63%.
So it is intermediate, the kind that makes andesite.

blocks.title: Mixing two magmas
blocks.q: 3 parts of basalt magma (50% silica) mix with 1 part of rhyolite magma (74% silica). What is the mixture?
steps: Weighted average: $\dfrac{3 \times 50 + 1 \times 74}{4} = \dfrac{224}{4} = 56\%$.
56% is intermediate. Mixing is one of the ways andesite forms at subduction zones.

blocks.html: It is easy to think the hottest lava must be the most explosive. Basalt is the hottest magma, and it usually erupts gently because it is runny and its gas escapes easily. Cooler, silica-rich magma traps gas and can explode. Check with two famous volcanoes: Kīlauea's hot basalt flows quietly; Mount St. Helens' cooler dacite blew apart in 1980.

blocks.html: Every igneous rock answers two questions. Which magma was it? That is its composition, from mafic to felsic. How fast did it cool? That is its texture, the size of its crystals. A simple grid of the two names most igneous rocks.

Crystals grow as atoms move through the melt and attach to them. Deep underground, magma is wrapped in hot rock and may take thousands to millions of years to cool, so a few crystals grow large: a coarse-grained (intrusive) rock. At the surface, lava cools in days to years, so countless tiny crystals start at once and none grows large: a fine-grained (extrusive) rock. Quench lava in seconds and atoms have no time to line up at all: glass. Two-stage cooling, slow and then fast, leaves big crystals in a fine background: porphyritic.

blocks.html: Texture tells where a rock cooled; composition tells which magma it was. Granite and rhyolite are the same felsic magma, cooled slowly underground or quickly at the surface; diorite–andesite and gabbro–basalt are the other pairs.

blocks.name: es-rock-key
blocks.cap: The igneous rock key: each cell shows a hand sample. Find granite and rhyolite: same column, different rows.

blocks.title: Name the rock
blocks.q: A rock has large, interlocking crystals of pink feldspar, glassy quartz and a little black mica. What is it?
steps: Large, visible crystals: coarse-grained, so it cooled slowly underground.
Quartz and potassium feldspar: felsic.
Coarse + felsic = granite.

blocks.title: Same rock, different cooling
blocks.q: Basalt and gabbro are both made of pyroxene and calcium-rich plagioclase. Why do they look so different?
steps: Same minerals means the same (mafic) magma.
Gabbro cooled slowly deep in the crust, growing crystals several millimeters across. Basalt cooled quickly as lava, so its crystals are too small to see.
blocks.a: They differ only in cooling rate.

blocks.name: es-igneous
blocks.cap: Cool the same magma in a deep pluton, a shallow dike, on land or in water, and compare the crystal sizes.

blocks.html: Naming a rock by color alone is a common trap. Dark rocks are often mafic, but obsidian is black glass with a felsic composition, and a dark, fine-grained rock could be basalt or andesite. Check both features: look for crystal size first (where it cooled), then for which minerals or how much silica (which magma).

Most magma never reaches the surface. It stalls underground and freezes into coarse-grained igneous rock in bodies called intrusions, or plutons, which we see only after erosion strips away the rock above. In Cross-Cutting Relationships you learned that whatever cuts across rock is younger than it; intrusions are the classic example. Their names describe their shape and how they relate to the layers around them.

items: Dike: a sheet of magma that cut across the layers (discordant), filling a crack.
Sill: a sheet that squeezed in between layers, parallel to them (concordant).
Laccolith: a sill-like body that bulged the layers above it into a dome.
Batholith: a huge pluton exposed over more than 100 km², often granite, the roots of old mountain ranges such as the Sierra Nevada. Smaller ones are stocks.
Volcanic neck: magma frozen in a volcano's throat, left standing when the softer cone eroded.

blocks.html: Magma rises because it is lighter than the rock around it. It pushes into cracks, so where the crust is being stretched it forms upright dikes; where the layers above are weaker to lift than to split, it spreads sideways between them as sills. Hot magma also bakes the rock it touches, a narrow zone of contact metamorphism. That baking is a clue to the age order.

Intrusions are named by shape: dikes cut across layers, sills run between them, and batholiths are huge bodies exposed over more than 100 km². An intrusion is younger than every rock it cuts or bakes.

blocks.name: es-strata
blocks.cap: Step through the history: a sill squeezes between layers, a lava flow spreads on the surface and is buried, then a dike cuts everything. Look at which sides of each body are baked.

blocks.title: Sill or buried lava flow?
blocks.q: A basalt layer lies between two sandstones. The sandstone above and below it is baked, and the basalt has no gas holes. Sill or lava flow?
steps: A lava flow cools at the surface: it bakes only the ground under it, and gas bubbles collect at its top.
A sill is injected between layers that were already there, so it bakes both.
Both sides are baked and there are no bubbles: it is a sill, younger than the sandstone above it.

blocks.title: Batholith or stock?
blocks.q: A granite body is exposed over an area about 9 km by 14 km. Batholith or stock?
steps: Area: $9 \times 14 = 126\,\text{km}^2$.
More than 100 km², so it is called a batholith.

blocks.html: A sill is easy to mistake for a buried lava flow: both are flat sheets of igneous rock between layers. But the order of events is different. A lava flow is older than the layer on top of it; a sill is younger than both its neighbors. Check the contacts: baked on both sides means sill; baked below only, with a bubbly, weathered top, means lava flow.

In Kinds of Volcanoes you met shield volcanoes, cinder cones and composite volcanoes. Their shapes come from how they erupt, and how they erupt comes down to two properties of the magma: its viscosity and its gas.

Deep underground, magma holds gases (mostly water vapor and carbon dioxide) dissolved under pressure, like the carbon dioxide in an unopened soda. As magma rises, the pressure drops and bubbles form. In runny basalt the bubbles rise and escape easily, so lava fountains and flows: a gentle, effusive eruption. In sticky andesite, dacite or rhyolite, bubbles can't escape. Pressure builds until the magma is torn apart into ash and pumice by expanding gas: an explosive eruption. Water expands about 1,700 times when it turns to steam, so even basalt explodes when it meets groundwater or the sea.

Viscosity and gas decide the style: runny, gas-poor basalt oozes out as lava; sticky, gas-rich felsic magma explodes as ash. The Volcanic Explosivity Index (VEI) rates eruptions by erupted volume, about ten times more for each step from VEI 2 up.

blocks.title: Comparing eruptions
blocks.q: About how many times more material does a VEI 6 eruption throw out than a VEI 4?
steps: Two steps, each about ×10.
$10 \times 10 = 100$ times.

blocks.title: Rating an eruption
blocks.q: An eruption throws out about 3 km³ of ash and rock. What is its VEI?
steps: VEI 5 starts at 1 km³ and VEI 6 at 10 km³.
3 km³ is between them: VEI 5.

blocks.html: The volcano with the biggest lava flows is not the most dangerous. Kīlauea pours out huge volumes of runny lava, but gently, and people can usually move out of its way. Mount St. Helens erupted far less lava, but its sticky, gas-rich magma blasted out explosively in 1980. Check the magma, not the volume: sticky plus gassy means explosive.

blocks.html: Eruption styles explain how volcanoes erupt. To protect people, scientists also need to know what each eruption does to the land around it, how far each hazard can reach, and how to tell when a volcano is waking up.

items: Pyroclastic flows: avalanches of hot ash, rock and gas, hundreds of degrees Celsius, racing downhill often faster than 80 km/h. They are the deadliest volcanic hazard.

Lahars: volcanic mudflows of water, ash and rock that flow down river valleys like wet concrete, sometimes tens of kilometers from the volcano. Melting snow, heavy rain or a burst crater lake can start them, even without an eruption.
Ash fall: fine particles of rock and glass, heavy when wet, that collapse roofs, ruin crops and damage jet engines far downwind.
Volcanic gases: sulfur dioxide makes acid rain and haze; carbon dioxide, heavier than air, can pool in low places.
Lava flows: usually slow enough to walk away from, but they bury whatever they reach.

blocks.html: Hazards follow physics. Hot flows are denser than air, so gravity drives them down valleys; that is also where lahars go, because they are mostly water. Wind decides where ash falls. Monitoring works because magma has to make room for itself as it rises: it pushes the ground up (swelling measured by GPS and tilt meters), cracks rock (swarms of small earthquakes), and releases gas as the pressure falls (more sulfur dioxide).

Each hazard reaches a different distance: pyroclastic flows and lava near the volcano, lahars far down river valleys, ash far downwind. Swelling ground, small earthquakes and changing gases warn that magma is moving.

blocks.name: es-volcano
blocks.cap: Hazard zones around a composite volcano: flows follow the valleys, and ash falls downwind.

blocks.title: How much warning?
blocks.q: A lahar races down a valley at 30 km/h. How long until it reaches a town 45 km away?
steps: Time = distance ÷ speed $= 45 \div 30 = 1.5\,\text{h}$, or 90 minutes.

In 1985, lahars from Nevado del Ruiz in Colombia took roughly two and a half hours to reach Armero, about 74 km away, and killed more than 20,000 people. Today, lahar warning systems give towns time to move to high ground.

blocks.title: Reading swelling ground
blocks.q: GPS shows the ground on a volcano rising 9 cm in 3 months. At that rate, how much in a year?
steps: $9 \div 3 = 3\,\text{cm per month}$.
$3 \times 12 = 36\,\text{cm}$ in a year: a strong sign that magma is collecting below.

blocks.html: It is tempting to think a volcano that has been quiet for centuries is dead. Many dangerous volcanoes rest hundreds or thousands of years between eruptions. Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines had been quiet for about 500 years before it erupted in 1991, one of the largest eruptions of the 20th century; monitoring gave enough warning for large evacuations. Check the record, not the calendar: a volcano that erupted in the last 10,000 years is generally treated as active.

blocks.html: In What Speeds Up Weathering you saw that warmth, water and surface area speed up the breakdown of rock. Now we look at the chemistry itself. Rain is not pure water: it dissolves a little carbon dioxide from the air and becomes weak carbonic acid, $\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2 \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$, with a pH near 5.6. Slowly, steadily, that acid takes rock apart.

items: Hydrolysis: water and its $\text{H}^{+}$ ions attack feldspar, the most common mineral in the crust, and rebuild it as clay: $2\text{KAlSi}_3\text{O}_8 + 2\text{H}^{+} + 9\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Al}_2\text{Si}_2\text{O}_5(\text{OH})_4 + 2\text{K}^{+} + 4\text{H}_4\text{SiO}_4$.
Oxidation: iron in olivine, pyroxene and biotite loses an electron to oxygen, $\text{Fe}^{2+} \rightarrow \text{Fe}^{3+}$, and forms rusty iron oxides that stain soil red and brown.

Dissolution: calcite dissolves completely in carbonic acid, $\text{CaCO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2 \rightarrow \text{Ca}^{2+} + 2\text{HCO}_3^{-}$. Underground this carves caves and sinkholes, a landscape called karst.

blocks.html: Minerals are most stable near the conditions where they formed. Bowen's series runs from olivine, formed at about $1,200^\circ\text{C}$ with no water, to quartz, formed at the cool end. At Earth's cool, wet surface, olivine is far from home and breaks down fastest; quartz, closest to surface conditions and with no iron to rust, barely changes. The weathering order (the Goldich series) is Bowen's series turned upside down.
Weak carbonic acid turns feldspar into clay, rusts iron minerals and dissolves calcite. Minerals that crystallize first from magma weather fastest; quartz weathers slowest, so it piles up as sand.

blocks.name: es-weathering
blocks.cap: Try each process in each climate. Chemical weathering is fastest where it is warm and wet.

blocks.title: Balance a dissolution
blocks.q: Balance: $\square\,\text{CaCO}_3 + \square\,\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3 \rightarrow \square\,\text{Ca}^{2+} + \square\,\text{HCO}_3^{-}$.
steps: Calcium: one on each side, so start with $1\,\text{CaCO}_3$ and $1\,\text{Ca}^{2+}$.
Carbon: $1 + 1 = 2$ on the left, so $2\,\text{HCO}_3^{-}$.
Check hydrogen: 2 on each side. Oxygen: $3 + 3 = 6 = 2 \times 3$. Charge: $0 = +2 - 2$.

blocks.title: A fading gravestone
blocks.q: In a rainy city, a marble gravestone loses about 1.5 mm of its surface per century. How much after 250 years?
steps: Per year: $1.5 \div 100 = 0.015\,\text{mm}$.
$0.015 \times 250 = 3.75\,\text{mm}$, enough to blur carved letters.

blocks.html: It seems logical that the minerals that crystallize first, at the highest temperatures, must be the toughest. At the surface it is the reverse: olivine weathers fastest and quartz lasts longest. Check with a beach: its sand is mostly quartz, even where the rocks upstream are full of feldspar and dark minerals.

blocks.html: The grains of sedimentary rocks come in every size, from clay too small to see to boulders bigger than a car. Size matters because it records how much energy moved the grains. Geologists sort sizes into classes on the Wentworth scale, where each class limit doubles or halves: 2 mm, 4 mm, 1/16 mm, and so on. That makes it a natural fit for logarithms.

Diameter (mm)
φ
blocks.cap: The Wentworth grain-size scale with phi values.

blocks.html: Because the class limits are powers of 2, a base-2 logarithm turns them into whole numbers. The phi scale is $\varphi = -\log_2 d$, with $d$ in millimeters. A 4 mm pebble is $2^2$ mm, so $\varphi = -2$; fine sand of $\tfrac18 = 2^{-3}$ mm has $\varphi = 3$. The minus sign was chosen so that the sand, silt and clay geologists measure most often get positive numbers. The log also makes it easy to average and compare sizes that differ a thousandfold.
$\varphi = -\log_2 d$ ($d$ in mm), and $d = 2^{-\varphi}$. Each step of 1 in phi halves or doubles the size. Coarse grains have small or negative phi; fine grains have large phi.

blocks.name: es-sediment
blocks.cap: The grain-size axis with phi values shown. Notice that phi increases to the left, toward finer grains.

blocks.title: Size to phi
blocks.q: What is $\varphi$ for a grain $\tfrac{1}{16}$ mm across?
steps: $\varphi = -\log_2 2^{-4} = -(-4) = 4$: the boundary between sand and silt.

blocks.title: Phi to size, with a calculator
blocks.q: What is $\varphi$ for a grain 0.3 mm across?
steps: $\varphi = 1.74$: medium sand.

blocks.html: It is natural to expect phi to grow with grain size, the way most measurements do. Because of the minus sign, it does the opposite: a boulder has $\varphi$ around $-9$ and clay around $9$. Check: a 1 mm grain has $\varphi = 0$; anything bigger is negative.

In Erosion and Deposition you saw that fast water carries sediment and slow water drops it. Here we make that precise, using the grain sizes from the last lesson. In 1935 Filip Hjulström plotted, for each grain size, how fast a river must flow to pick grains up and how slow it must get before they settle. His diagram has three fields: erosion, transport and deposition.

Moving water drags on a grain. For sand and gravel, bigger grains are heavier, so they need faster water to lift. You might expect the curve to keep falling for smaller grains, but it turns back up: silt and clay particles stick together and pack into a smooth bed that the current slides over, so it takes fast water to tear them loose. Settling is different. A tiny grain sinks very slowly, because its weight shrinks faster than the drag on it: by Stokes' law, $v = \dfrac{(\rho_s - \rho_w) g d^2}{18\mu}$, so halving the size cuts the settling speed by four. Once lifted, clay stays suspended in water that barely moves.

Faster water moves bigger grains, but the easiest grains to erode are fine-to-medium sand (about 0.1 to 0.5 mm). Clay is hard to erode but, once moving, settles so slowly that almost any current keeps it suspended.

blocks.cap: The Hjulström diagram. Drag the point: grain size across, flow speed up. Which field does it fall in?

blocks.title: Picked up or dropped?
blocks.q: Water flowing at 5 cm/s passes over loose gravel 20 mm across. What happens to the gravel?
steps: On the diagram, 20 mm gravel needs about 130 cm/s to be lifted from the bed, and moving gravel drops out below about 90 cm/s.
5 cm/s is far below both, so the point lies in the deposition field: the gravel stays put (or drops, if it was moving).
blocks.a: It is deposited; nothing moves it.

blocks.title: How slowly silt settles
blocks.q: A quartz silt grain 10 μm across ($d = 1 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{m}$, $\rho_s = 2,650\,\text{kg/m}^3$) settles in water ($\rho_w = 1,000$, $\mu = 0.001\,\text{Pa·s}$). How fast?
steps: $v \approx 9.0 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{m/s} = 0.09\,\text{mm/s}$: about 3 hours to sink one meter.

blocks.html: It is tempting to assume the smallest grains are always the easiest to pick up. Sticky clay and silt need faster water to erode than sand does. Check on the diagram: the erosion curve dips lowest near 0.2 to 0.5 mm and rises on both sides.

blocks.html: Pick up a handful of sand from a beach and one from a landslide, and you are holding two different histories. Moving water and weathering change sediment the longer they work on it, and three features record how long: sorting, rounding and composition.

items: Sorting: how alike the grain sizes are in one sample. Waves and wind carry away grains that are too fine and leave those too coarse, so beach and dune sand is well sorted. Glaciers and landslides dump everything together: poorly sorted.
Rounding: how worn the corners are. Grains knocking together lose their sharp edges, slowly, over long distances or many trips.
Composition: weathering destroys feldspar and dark minerals over time, while quartz survives. A sand that is over 90% quartz is mature.

blocks.html: Each feature measures time and energy. Sorting needs a process that picks grains by size again and again, like waves sloshing back and forth for years. Rounding needs countless collisions. Mineral maturity needs time for slow chemical reactions. So a well-sorted, well-rounded, quartz-rich sand has had a long, busy history, while an angular, poorly sorted, feldspar-rich one came quickly from a nearby source.
The farther and longer sediment travels, the better sorted and rounder it gets and the richer in quartz. Well sorted means the grains in one sample are about the same size.

blocks.name: es-sediment
blocks.cap: Slide the distance traveled from 0 to 200 km and watch the grains become rounder, better sorted and more quartz-rich.

blocks.title: Which traveled farther?
blocks.q: Sample X: angular grains of many sizes, about half feldspar. Sample Y: rounded, well-sorted grains, nearly all quartz. Which traveled farther?
steps: Rounding, sorting and quartz-richness all grow with transport.
Y shows all three; X shows none. Y traveled farther; X probably came from granite close by.

blocks.title: Counting quartz
blocks.q: Of 400 grains counted under a microscope, 372 are quartz. Mature or immature?
steps: Over 90%: a mature quartz sand.

blocks.html: "Well sorted" sounds as if the sediment were sorted into separate layers. It means something else: within one sample, the grains are nearly all the same size. A single thin layer of dune sand is well sorted; a thick, layered pile of glacial till is still poorly sorted. Check by looking at one handful, not at the layers.

Sedimentary rocks form in two ways, and the first question in naming one is which way. Clastic rocks are piles of broken grains, the sediment of earlier rocks, pressed and cemented together. Chemical and biochemical rocks grow from minerals dissolved in water, either crystallizing as water evaporates or built into the shells and skeletons of living things.

blocks.cap: Clastic rocks are named by grain size (and, for gravel, shape); the others by what they are made of.

blocks.html: Names follow how the rock formed. For clastic rocks, grain size is the record of energy, so it comes first; for gravel, shape adds a clue about distance, since rounded gravel traveled and angular gravel did not. For chemical rocks, the mineral tells the story: calcite means life in warm seas, halite and gypsum mean water evaporated, plant carbon means a swamp. Turning loose sediment into rock is called lithification: burial packs the grains (compaction), and minerals such as calcite or quartz crystallize between them as cement.

Clastic rocks are named by grain size, and gravel rocks by shape: conglomerate, breccia, sandstone, siltstone, shale. Chemical and biochemical rocks are named by composition: limestone, rock salt, rock gypsum, chert, coal.

blocks.cap: The sedimentary rock key. Compare conglomerate and breccia: same size, different shape.

blocks.title: Name a clastic rock
blocks.q: A rock is made of angular pieces of gravel, 5 to 30 mm, cemented together. Name it.
steps: Over 2 mm: gravel, so conglomerate or breccia.
Angular pieces: breccia. The sharp corners mean they did not travel far, perhaps from a rockfall or fault zone.

blocks.title: Name a chemical rock
blocks.q: A gray rock fizzes in dilute acid and holds broken shells. Name it.
steps: Fizzing in acid means calcite.
Calcite with shells: limestone, a biochemical rock.

blocks.html: Many people picture limestone as sand cemented together. Most limestone is calcite, built by corals, shellfish and microscopic algae in warm, shallow seas and later cemented. Check with acid: limestone fizzes; a quartz sandstone does not.

Sediment records not only what it is made of, but how it was laid down. Ripples, cracks and slanting layers frozen into sedimentary rock tell which way water flowed, whether waves were sloshing, whether the mud dried in the air, and even which way was up when the layer formed.

items: Cross-beds: sloping layers inside a thicker bed, left as ripples or dunes migrated. Sand rolls up the gentle upstream side and avalanches down the steep front, so the cross-beds dip in the direction the current or wind was moving.
Ripple marks: lopsided (asymmetric) ripples come from a current flowing one way, their steep side facing downstream. Even, symmetric ripples come from waves sloshing back and forth.
Mud cracks: wet mud dried in the air, shrank and cracked into polygons, wide at the top and narrowing downward.
Graded beds: coarse at the bottom, fine at the top, left when a muddy flow (such as an underwater turbidity current) slowed and its grains settled, biggest first.

blocks.html: Each structure is made by a process that has a direction in time and space. Gravity settles coarse grains before fine ones, so a graded bed's coarse end was at the bottom; mud dries from the top, so cracks narrow downward; cross-beds are cut off at their tops and curve out at their bottoms. That lets geologists tell whether a layer has been turned upside down, which happens in tight folds.

Cross-beds and asymmetric ripples show which way a current flowed (toward their steep side); symmetric ripples show waves; mud cracks show drying in the air; graded beds and mud cracks show which way was up.

blocks.name: es-sediment
blocks.cap: Watch dunes migrate and leave cross-beds. Switch structures, and try turning a layer upside down.

blocks.title: Which way did it flow?
blocks.q: Asymmetric ripples in a sandstone have their steep sides facing southeast. Which way did the current flow?
steps: Sand climbs the gentle side and tumbles down the steep side.
So the current flowed toward the steep side: to the southeast.

blocks.title: Which way is up?
blocks.q: In a cliff, a layer of sandstone is fine-grained at the bottom and coarse at the top. What happened?
steps: A graded bed settles coarse first, so it should be coarse at the bottom.
This one is the other way around: the rocks have been folded and overturned.

blocks.html: Reading every ripple the same way is a common slip. Symmetric ripples, with matching slopes, come from waves moving water back and forth; they do not show a current direction. Only lopsided ripples do, with the steep side downstream. Check the two slopes before you read a direction.

Every place where sediment collects leaves a fingerprint. Combine structures, sorting and rounding, rock type and fossils, and you can name the environment a rock formed in, even if that place vanished hundreds of millions of years ago.

head: Environment
Typical rocks and clues
rows: channels of conglomerate and cross-bedded sandstone; red floodplain mudstone with mud cracks and roots
sand at the mouth grading out to mud; plant remains; layers building seaward
well-sorted, rounded quartz sand; gentle seaward-dipping layers; shell fragments
limestone with corals and shells, often in growth position
thin layers of dark shale; fossils of floating organisms; no current marks
thick, well-sorted sandstone; huge cross-beds; frosted, rounded grains
