blocks.cap: Clues to the main depositional environments.

blocks.html: Each environment has its own energy and chemistry. High energy (rivers, beaches) moves sand and gravel and washes away mud; quiet water (deep sea, lagoons) lets clay settle; warm, clear shallow seas let reef builders thrive; dry heat evaporates water and leaves salts. Neighboring environments also lie side by side: going out to sea, beach sand gives way to offshore mud and then to deeper limestone. When sea level rises, those belts shift inland and stack on top of one another, so a vertical sequence records how the shoreline moved.

Rocks keep a record of where they formed: grain size and sorting show energy, structures show how water or wind moved, fossils show who lived there. Deeper-water rocks stacked on shallower ones mean the sea rose.

blocks.name: es-sediment
blocks.cap: Where a river meets still water, sediment sorts by size outward: one landscape, several environments side by side.

blocks.title: Name the environment
blocks.q: A thick sandstone is made of well-sorted, frosted, rounded quartz grains in cross-beds several meters high. Where did it form?
steps: Well sorted and frosted: sorted and pitted by wind.
Cross-beds meters high: big migrating dunes.
A desert sand sea, like the Navajo Sandstone of Utah.

blocks.title: Reading a sequence
blocks.q: Going up through the layers: beach sandstone, then offshore shale, then limestone. What happened?
steps: Each layer formed in deeper water than the one below.
So the sea rose and the shoreline moved inland: a transgression.

blocks.html: It is natural to think a rock formed where it is found today. Marine limestone with fossil shells sits near the top of Mount Everest; it formed on an ancient seafloor and was lifted more than 8 km when India collided with Asia. Check the fossils and structures, not today's setting.

Metamorphism is change without melting: rock buried deep enough is heated and squeezed until its minerals rebuild themselves. To understand it we need numbers for how hot and how squeezed rock gets with depth. Temperature comes from the geothermal gradient; pressure comes from the weight of the rock above, the same idea as water pressure in a pool, using a formula we can rearrange.

Picture a column of rock 1 m² across and $h$ meters tall. Its mass is $\rho \times h$ (density times volume), its weight is $\rho g h$, and that weight spreads over 1 m², so the pressure at the bottom is $P = \rho g h$. For crust of $2,700\,\text{kg/m}^3$: $2,700 \times 9.8 \times 1,000 \approx 26,000,000\,\text{Pa}$ per kilometer, about 26 MPa per km. Geologists also use kilobars: $1\,\text{kbar} = 100\,\text{MPa}$, so the pressure grows about 1 kbar every 3.8 km.

items: Confining pressure comes from the rock above and pushes equally from all sides. It squeezes rock smaller and denser but has no direction.

Differential (directed) stress pushes harder one way than another, as when plates collide. It flattens grains and makes platy minerals such as mica grow at right angles to the push, lining them up into foliation.

blocks.html: Pressure from overlying rock is $P = \rho g h$, about 26 MPa per kilometer in the crust; temperature rises along the geotherm. Equal pressure only compresses rock; foliation needs stronger squeezing in one direction.

blocks.name: es-interior
blocks.cap: Pressure and temperature with depth, with the zones where different kinds of metamorphism happen.

blocks.title: Pressure at 10 km
blocks.q: Rock averages $2,700\,\text{kg/m}^3$. What is the pressure 10 km down?
steps: That is 265 MPa, or 2.65 kbar: about 2,600 times the air pressure at sea level.

blocks.title: How deep was this schist?
blocks.q: Minerals in a schist show it formed at 6 kbar. The rock above averaged $2,800\,\text{kg/m}^3$. How deep was it?
steps: $6\,\text{kbar} = 600\,\text{MPa} = 6 \times 10^{8}\,\text{Pa}$.
$h = \dfrac{P}{\rho g} = \dfrac{6 \times 10^{8}}{2,800 \times 9.8} \approx 21,900\,\text{m}$.
About 22 km. The schist now at the surface was once buried that deep, under mountains long since worn away.

blocks.html: Many people think pressure alone lines minerals up into layers. Pressure that is equal on all sides, like water pressure on a diver, shrinks a rock but has no direction to line anything up along. Foliation needs directed stress, which is why foliated rocks mark old mountain belts where plates collided. Check: a deep pluton that cooled under huge but even pressure, like most granite, has no foliation.

sources.name: OpenStax, College Physics 2e, section 11.4, Variation of Pressure with Depth in a Fluid

blocks.html: In Metamorphic Rocks you saw shale become slate and granite become gneiss. Now we follow one rock up the ladder of heat and pressure. Metamorphic grade is how intensely a rock has been changed, and as pressure and temperature rise, the same shale passes through a series of new rocks and new minerals.

head: Grade
Rock from shale
What you see
Index mineral
rows: dull, fine-grained; splits into flat sheets
light and dark bands of coarse crystals
blocks.cap: Regional metamorphism of shale (temperatures rounded and approximate; they shift with pressure).

blocks.html: Clay minerals in shale are stable only at low temperature. As the rock heats, atoms rearrange into minerals that are stable at the new conditions. First, tiny micas grow, lined up by directed stress (slate). With more heat, they grow larger (phyllite, then schist). At high grade, light minerals (quartz, feldspar) and dark ones (biotite, amphibole) separate into bands (gneiss). Some minerals form only above a certain temperature, so their first appearance marks a grade: these are index minerals, mapped as lines across mountain belts since the 1890s in Scotland.
As heat and pressure rise, shale becomes slate, phyllite, schist, then gneiss, and index minerals appear in order: chlorite, biotite, garnet, staurolite, kyanite, sillimanite.

blocks.name: es-interior
blocks.cap: Index minerals appear one after another as temperature rises along a geotherm.

blocks.title: Which index mineral?
blocks.q: A shale reached about $520^\circ\text{C}$. Using the table, what is its highest-grade index mineral?
steps: 520 °C is past garnet (480 °C) but short of staurolite (560 °C).
So garnet is the highest-grade index mineral: it is a garnet schist.

blocks.title: How deep for garnet?
blocks.q: Garnet appears at about $480^\circ\text{C}$. With a surface of $15^\circ\text{C}$ and a gradient of $30^\circ\text{C/km}$, how deep must shale be buried?
steps: $480 - 15 = 465^\circ\text{C}$ of warming.

blocks.html: Slate, phyllite, schist and gneiss are often treated as four unrelated rocks. They can be one parent rock, shale, cooked to higher and higher grade, and in many mountain belts you can walk from one to the next. Check with the micas: their size grows steadily from slate to schist, the clue that it is one sequence.

To name a metamorphic rock, ask two questions. Is it foliated, with minerals lined up in layers or bands? And what was its parent rock? Metamorphism rebuilds the minerals but mostly keeps the chemistry, so the parent shows through. Metamorphic grade names the foliated rocks; the nonfoliated ones are named by their main mineral.

head: Parent rock
Metamorphic rock
Foliated?
blocks.cap: Common metamorphic rocks and their parents.

blocks.html: Foliation needs two things: platy or long minerals (micas, amphiboles) and directed stress to line them up. Shale is full of clay that turns into mica, so it foliates readily. Limestone is almost pure calcite and quartz sandstone almost pure quartz; neither makes platy minerals, so their crystals simply grow into an interlocking mosaic: marble and quartzite. In quartzite the grains are welded so tightly that a break runs straight through them; in sandstone, a break runs around the grains through the weaker cement.
Name a metamorphic rock by foliation and parent: foliated slate, phyllite, schist and gneiss; nonfoliated marble (from limestone), quartzite (from quartz sandstone) and hornfels (baked rock).

blocks.name: es-rock-key
blocks.cap: The metamorphic rock key: foliated rocks by grade, nonfoliated rocks by mineral.

blocks.title: Marble or quartzite?
blocks.q: A pale rock of interlocking crystals fizzes when a drop of dilute acid touches it. Name it and its parent.
steps: Fizzing in acid means calcite.
Interlocking calcite crystals: marble, from limestone.

blocks.title: From the parent
blocks.q: What does quartz sandstone become when metamorphosed?
steps: It is nearly all quartz, which forms no platy minerals.
The grains recrystallize and fuse: quartzite, a nonfoliated rock that scratches glass.

blocks.html: Quartzite and sandstone look alike: both are pale and made of quartz. The test is how they break. Sandstone breaks around its grains, and loose grains rub off on your fingers. Quartzite breaks right through its grains with a glassy surface, because metamorphism welded them together. Check with a hammer, or look closely at a broken edge.

Metamorphism needs heat, pressure or hot fluids, and different places on Earth supply them in different mixes. Knowing which rock formed and at what pressure and temperature lets geologists say where it formed, and even which kind of plate boundary once stood there.

items: Contact metamorphism: heat from an intrusion bakes the rock beside it in a zone (an aureole) meters to kilometers wide. High temperature, low pressure; it can happen just a few kilometers down. Makes hornfels and marble.

Regional metamorphism: when plates collide, huge regions of crust are buried, heated and squeezed together. Medium to high pressure and temperature, with directed stress. Makes slate, schist and gneiss.
Subduction-zone metamorphism: a cold ocean plate sinks faster than heat can warm it, so it meets high pressure at low temperature. Makes blueschist, colored by a blue amphibole.
Hydrothermal metamorphism: hot water circulating through rock, especially new ocean crust at ridges, changes its minerals.
Impact metamorphism: a meteorite strike delivers enormous pressure for an instant, leaving shocked quartz.

blocks.html: Each setting has its own ratio of temperature to depth. Divide a rock's formation temperature by its depth (from $P = \rho g h$): around $10^\circ\text{C/km}$ or less means rock went deep while staying cold, which happens only where a slab is sinking. About 20 to $35^\circ\text{C/km}$ is the normal heating of thickened crust in a mountain belt. Much higher means a heat source close by: magma.

Contact metamorphism bakes rock beside magma (hot, shallow); regional metamorphism comes with mountain building (hot and deep, with directed stress); subduction makes high-pressure, low-temperature rocks such as blueschist.

blocks.name: es-interior
blocks.cap: Metamorphic settings on a pressure–temperature chart: subduction along the cold, deep side; contact metamorphism along the hot, shallow side.

blocks.title: Reading the gradient
blocks.q: A rock formed at $350^\circ\text{C}$ and 1.2 GPa. With rock of $2,800\,\text{kg/m}^3$, what setting fits?
steps: Depth: $h = \dfrac{1.2 \times 10^9}{2,800 \times 9.8} \approx 43.7\,\text{km}$.
Gradient: $350 \div 43.7 \approx 8^\circ\text{C/km}$: very cold for its depth.
Only a sinking slab goes that deep while staying that cool: a subduction zone (blueschist conditions).

blocks.title: A baked zone
blocks.q: Shale changes to hornfels only within 300 m of a granite stock that cooled 3 km down. Which setting?
steps: The change is limited to a narrow zone around the intrusion, at shallow depth.
That is contact metamorphism: the heat came from the magma, not from deep burial.

blocks.html: It is easy to think all metamorphism needs deep burial. A hot intrusion can bake the rock beside it only a few kilometers down, or even right at the surface under a thick lava flow. Check the extent: metamorphism that fades within a zone around an intrusion is contact metamorphism, whatever the depth.

sources.name: USGS, This Dynamic Earth: The Story of Plate Tectonics (Kious and Tilling)

blocks.html: Plates push, pull and slide, and the rock between them has to respond. Two words keep the cause and the effect apart. Stress is the force per area acting on rock, like pressure but possibly stronger in one direction. Strain is the change in shape or size that results.

items: Compression squeezes rock together, shortening and thickening it: folds and reverse faults (colliding plates).
Tension pulls rock apart, stretching and thinning it: normal faults (rifts).
Shear pushes two sides past each other: strike-slip faults (transform boundaries).

blocks.html: Whether rock bends or breaks depends on conditions. Near the surface, rock is cold and the confining pressure is low, so cracks can open and grow: rock is brittle and fractures. Deep down, heat lets atoms move and pressure keeps cracks closed, so crystals slowly slide and regrow: rock is ductile and flows, folding like warm wax. Speed matters too: a slow push for millions of years favors bending; a sudden one favors breaking. In quartz-rich crust the change from brittle to ductile happens at about $300^\circ\text{C}$, typically 10 to 15 km down.

Stress (compression, tension or shear) causes strain. Shallow, cold rock under fast stress is brittle and breaks; deep, hot rock under slow stress is ductile and folds. Strain is measured as change in length ÷ original length.

blocks.name: es-structures
blocks.cap: The same push on cold, shallow rock and on hot, deep rock: one breaks, one bends.

blocks.title: Shortening a belt
blocks.q: A belt of rock layers 80 km wide is squeezed to 60 km. What is the strain?
steps: Change in length: $60 - 80 = -20\,\text{km}$.
Strain: $-20 \div 80 = -0.25$: shortened by $25\%$.
The rock didn't vanish: the belt got thicker as it got narrower, which is how mountains grow.

blocks.title: Where earthquakes stop
blocks.q: With a surface of $15^\circ\text{C}$ and a gradient of $25^\circ\text{C/km}$, how deep is the $300^\circ\text{C}$ brittle–ductile change?
steps: $300 - 15 = 285^\circ\text{C}$ of warming.
$285 \div 25 \approx 11.4\,\text{km}$.
That is why most earthquakes in continents start in the top 10 to 20 km.

blocks.html: It is natural to think solid rock can't bend. Given heat, pressure and time, it can: folded layers in mountain belts were bent while solid, never melted. Check a folded outcrop: the layers stay continuous around the bends, with no breaks, which only ductile flow can do.

sources.name: OpenStax, College Physics 2e, section 5.3, Elasticity: Stress and Strain

blocks.html: When compression acts on layered rock deep enough for it to be ductile, the layers bend into folds, like a rug pushed across a floor. Using superposition, we can recognize folds even after erosion has worn them flat.

items: Anticline: layers arch upward. Its limbs dip away from its middle line (the axis).
Syncline: layers sag downward. Its limbs dip toward the axis.
Dome and basin: an anticline or syncline that bends in every direction, round instead of long.
Plunging folds: the axis itself tilts, so eroded outcrops make V- or U-shaped patterns.

blocks.html: Before folding, the oldest layer was at the bottom. Arch the layers up and wear the top flat, and the cut exposes the deepest, oldest layers in the middle, with younger layers repeating on both sides in mirror image. Sag them down and erode, and the youngest layer is left in the middle of the trough. So the map pattern, not the shape of the land, tells the fold: oldest in the middle means anticline (or dome), youngest in the middle means syncline (or basin).
Anticlines arch up and synclines sag down. Once eroded, an anticline shows its oldest rocks in the middle and a syncline its youngest; domes and basins show the same patterns as rings.

blocks.name: es-structures
blocks.cap: A folded block with its top worn flat. Change the fold type and the erosion, and watch the pattern on the top surface.

blocks.title: Read the map
blocks.q: Walking east across a plain, you cross rocks aged 300, 320, 350, 320 and 300 million years. What fold is it?
steps: The ages are a mirror image around the middle: a fold.
The oldest rock (350) is in the middle.
Oldest in the middle means an anticline.

blocks.title: How much shortening?
blocks.q: Measured along its curves, a folded bed is 20 km long, but it now spans only 15 km. How much was the crust shortened?
steps: Before folding the bed was flat and 20 km long.

blocks.html: It is tempting to assume an anticline is a hill and a syncline a valley. Erosion often wears the land flat, and the broken, stretched crest of an anticline can even erode into a valley. Check the rocks, not the landscape: find which layers are oldest, and see whether they sit in the middle.

Where rock is brittle, stress makes it break. A fault is a break along which the rock on one side has moved past the other. Faults are named by which way the blocks moved, and that tells you which stress made them.

On a sloping fault, the block above the fault plane is the hanging wall and the block below is the footwall (miners named them: you stand on the footwall and hang your lantern from the hanging wall). Pull the crust apart and the hanging wall slides down the slope; the crust gets longer. Push the crust together and the hanging wall is shoved up the slope; the crust gets shorter and thicker. Shear the crust sideways and the blocks slide past each other horizontally.

head: Fault
Motion
Stress
Example
rows: hanging wall up, fault dipping under about 30°
blocks.cap: The main kinds of faults.

blocks.html: Name a fault by how the hanging wall moved relative to the footwall: down for normal (tension), up for reverse and thrust (compression). Strike-slip faults move sideways; looking across one, if the far side moved right, it is right-lateral.

blocks.name: es-structures
blocks.cap: Slip the fault and watch the layers and the road offset. Switch fault types.

blocks.title: Throw and heave
blocks.q: A normal fault dips $60^\circ$. The hanging wall slid 40 m down the fault plane. How far did it drop vertically, and how far did the crust stretch?
steps: The slip is the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose angle is the dip.
Vertical (throw): $40 \sin 60^\circ = 40 \times 0.866 \approx 34.6\,\text{m}$.
Horizontal (heave): $40 \cos 60^\circ = 40 \times 0.5 = 20\,\text{m}$ of stretching.
blocks.a: About 34.6 m down and 20 m of stretching.

blocks.title: Which side moved?
blocks.q: Standing on one side of a strike-slip fault, you see a fence on the far side offset 3 m to your left. What kind of fault?
steps: Looking across the fault, the far side moved left.
That is left-lateral, and a person on the other side would also see your side moved to their left.

blocks.html: A common slip is to decide a fault's type by which side stands higher today. Erosion can wear the raised side down, or the land may be flat. The type is set by how the hanging wall moved compared with the footwall: follow a matching layer across the fault. Check: if the same layer is lower on the hanging wall side, it is a normal fault, whatever the landscape looks like.

sources.name: USGS, This Dynamic Earth: The Story of Plate Tectonics (Kious and Tilling)

blocks.html: To map folded or tilted rock, geologists describe each layer's orientation with two measurements, strike and dip. With right-triangle trigonometry they then predict where the layer goes underground: how deep to drill for a coal seam or an aquifer.

items: Strike: the compass direction of a horizontal line on the tilted layer. Imagine the layer meeting a perfectly flat lake: the shoreline runs along the strike.
Dip: how steeply the layer slopes down from horizontal, measured at a right angle to the strike, and the direction it slopes. Water poured on the layer would run straight down the dip.

blocks.html: On a tilted plane, every direction slopes a different amount, but only one is horizontal (the strike) and only one is steepest (the dip direction), and the two are always at right angles. In the vertical slice that points down the dip, the layer is a straight line at the dip angle $\delta$. Walk a horizontal distance $x$ from where it crops out, and the layer lies a depth $d$ below you, the opposite side of a right triangle: $d = x\tan\delta$. A layer cropping out in a band $w$ wide on level ground has true thickness $t = w\sin\delta$.
Strike is the compass direction of a level line on a tilted layer; dip is its downward slope, at right angles to the strike. Down the dip, depth $= x\tan(\text{dip})$.

blocks.name: es-structures
blocks.cap: A tilted layer with its strike line and dip symbol. Change the dip and the well distance, and watch the depth.

blocks.title: How deep to drill?
blocks.q: A coal seam crops out on level ground, strikes north–south and dips $25^\circ$ east. How deep is it under a point 300 m east of the outcrop?
steps: East is straight down the dip, so use $d = x\tan\delta$.
$d = 300 \tan 25^\circ = 300 \times 0.466 \approx 140\,\text{m}$.

blocks.title: Which way does it dip?
blocks.q: A layer strikes N40°E (azimuth $40^\circ$) and dips to the southeast. What is its dip direction as an azimuth?
steps: The dip direction is $90^\circ$ from the strike: $40^\circ + 90^\circ = 130^\circ$ or $40^\circ - 90^\circ = 310^\circ$.
Southeast is $130^\circ$ (S50°E).

blocks.html: It is easy to draw the dip direction along the strike, or at some random angle. Dip always points straight down the slope, at a right angle to the strike. Check by picturing water on the layer: it runs downhill perpendicular to the level shoreline, never along it.

In Cross-Cutting Relationships and Fossils you began reading rock layers in order. In 1669 Nicolas Steno wrote down the rules that make it possible, and two centuries of geologists added more. Together they let you order the events in any outcrop without a single number.

head: Principle
What it says
rows: In undisturbed layers, each layer is younger than the one below it.
Sediment settles in flat, horizontal layers; tilted or folded layers were disturbed later.
Layers spread sideways until they thin out, so matching layers across a canyon were once joined.
A dike, fault or erosion surface is younger than the rock it cuts.
Pieces of one rock inside another are older than the rock that holds them.
Fossils appear in a definite order through the layers, so a fossil assemblage marks a span of time.
blocks.cap: The principles of relative dating.

blocks.html: Each principle is physics or biology. Gravity settles grains in flat sheets, oldest at the bottom. A crack can only cut rock that is already there, and a pebble can only be eroded from rock that already existed. Species appear and go extinct once, never to return, so the order of fossils is the same everywhere; William Smith used this around 1800 to match layers across England.

Read layers bottom to top (superposition), remember that layers start flat (original horizontality) and continuous (lateral continuity), and place anything that cuts across or is included in them in its proper turn (cross-cutting, inclusions). Fossils order layers everywhere.

blocks.name: es-strata
blocks.cap: Step through the history of this cross-section one event at a time, then turn on letters to test yourself.

blocks.title: Which is older?
blocks.q: Sandstone sits on top of granite. Rounded pebbles of the granite are found in the bottom of the sandstone, and the granite at the contact is not baked. Which is older?
steps: Inclusions: the granite pebbles in the sandstone must have existed before the sandstone.
No baking: the granite was not hot magma when the sand arrived; it had cooled, been exposed and eroded.
So the granite is older.

blocks.title: Tilted layers
blocks.q: Layers of sandstone and shale stand at $40^\circ$. What happened, and in what order?
steps: Original horizontality: the layers were laid down flat.
So first they were deposited, oldest at the bottom, then later tilted by folding or faulting.

blocks.html: It is natural to think tilted layers were laid down tilted. Loose sediment can't build steep layers over large areas; it settles in nearly flat sheets. So steep layers record a later event. Check: cross-beds are the small, local exception, and they are cut off at the top by the next flat layer.

Superposition assumes layers pile up without a break. Often they don't. For long stretches of time, rock was worn away, or none was laid down at all, and then deposition began again. The buried erosion surface between the older and younger rocks is an unconformity: a gap in the record.

items: Angular unconformity: older layers were tilted or folded, eroded flat, then buried by new, flat layers. The angle between them is the giveaway.
Nonconformity: sedimentary layers rest on eroded igneous or metamorphic rock, which formed deep underground and had to be uplifted and exposed first.
Disconformity: layers above and below are parallel, so only an uneven erosion surface, sometimes with pebbles or old soil along it, reveals the gap.

blocks.html: Each kind tells a story. An angular unconformity needs deposition, then deformation, then uplift and erosion, then sinking and more deposition, a long history squeezed into one surface. A nonconformity means kilometers of rock were stripped away to expose a pluton or schist. Their time gaps can be huge: in the Grand Canyon, the Great Unconformity separates rocks hundreds of millions to more than a billion years apart.

An unconformity is a buried erosion surface that marks missing time, not a layer. It is angular (tilted rocks below), a nonconformity (igneous or metamorphic rock below) or a disconformity (parallel layers).

blocks.name: es-strata
blocks.cap: Build an angular unconformity: deposit, tilt, erode, deposit again. The dashed line is the buried erosion surface.

blocks.title: What kind?
blocks.q: Horizontal limestone sits on an uneven surface of schist and gneiss. What kind of unconformity?
steps: Schist and gneiss are metamorphic rocks, formed deep underground.
Sedimentary rock on eroded metamorphic rock is a nonconformity.

blocks.title: How much time is missing?
blocks.q: The youngest layer below an unconformity is 410 million years old; the oldest layer above it is 320 million years old. How much time does the surface represent?
steps: $410 - 320 = 90$ million years.
For 90 million years, rock was eroded here, or never deposited.

blocks.html: Many students think an unconformity is a special kind of layer. It is a surface, a gap: the rock that would have recorded that time is missing. Check the ages: across a normal layer boundary the ages change smoothly; across an unconformity they jump.

One outcrop shows only part of Earth's history. To build a longer record, geologists match layers from place to place, called correlation. Lateral continuity says a layer once ran continuously, so matching its pieces across a valley or a continent ties their histories together.

items: Rock type: matching sandstone to sandstone works over short distances, where a layer can be traced.
Key beds: a distinctive layer laid down in a geologic instant over a wide area, such as volcanic ash, is a time marker.
Index fossils: species that lived a short time, spread widely and were common mark a narrow span of time wherever they are found.

blocks.html: The same kind of rock can form many times: sand piles up on every beach in every age. So rock type alone can match layers of different ages. A key bed or an index fossil, on the other hand, marks a moment or a short span of time. When a layer holds two fossils, it formed while both species were alive, inside the overlap of their ranges, which narrows the age further.
Correlate layers by rock type over short distances, and by key beds (such as ash) and index fossils over long ones. A layer with several fossils formed where their time ranges overlap.

blocks.name: es-strata
blocks.cap: Three rock columns from different places. Use the ash bed and the fossils to draw tie lines between matching layers.

blocks.title: Overlapping ranges
blocks.q: Fossil X lived from 480 to 440 million years ago; fossil Y from 460 to 420. A shale holds both. When did it form?
steps: Both lived only during the overlap.
The overlap begins when Y appeared, 460, and ends when X died out, 440.
So the shale formed between 460 and 440 million years ago.

blocks.title: Good index fossil?
blocks.q: A species of clam lived for 200 million years in seas worldwide. Is it a good index fossil?
steps: It was widespread and common, but its range is huge.
Finding it only says "sometime in a 200-million-year span": a poor index fossil.

blocks.html: Matching layers by color or thickness alone is a common trap. Two red sandstones at two sites can be tens of millions of years apart. Check with time markers: a shared ash bed or index fossil is far stronger evidence than look-alike rock.
Now put the principles together. A cross-section is a puzzle with every piece showing: layers, folds, faults, intrusions and unconformities. Your job is to list the events in the order they happened.

items: Start at the bottom: the oldest layers came first (superposition).
If those layers are tilted or folded, the deformation came after them (original horizontality).
An erosion surface that cuts across them came after the deformation; the layers resting on it came after the erosion.

Anything that cuts across rock comes after what it cuts: a dike after the layers it crosses, a fault after every layer it offsets. If a dike stops at an unconformity, it was cut off by the erosion, so it came before it.

blocks.html: Every rule is a "this had to exist before that" statement, and together they put the events in a chain. Order matters for more than tidiness: a fault that cuts every layer could still move; one buried under an unconformity has been quiet for as long as the rocks above it. Geologists reconstruct histories like this to find water, oil and ores, and to judge hazards.

Work from the bottom up, then insert deformation, erosion and cutting features in their turn: a feature is younger than everything it cuts or rests on, and older than everything that cuts it or covers it.

blocks.name: es-strata
blocks.cap: Replay this history: four layers, tilting, a dike, erosion, two new layers, then a fault. Turn on letters and order them yourself before stepping through.

blocks.title: Order the events
blocks.q: From the bottom: sandstone, shale, limestone, siltstone, all tilted. A dike cuts them and stops at an erosion surface. Conglomerate and sandstone lie flat on the surface. A fault offsets everything. Order the events.
steps: Sandstone, shale, limestone, siltstone were deposited, oldest at the bottom.
They were tilted; the dike cut them; the erosion surface truncated both.
Conglomerate, then sandstone, were deposited on the erosion surface.
The fault offsets every layer, so it came last.
blocks.a: Four layers, tilting, dike, erosion, two layers, fault.

blocks.title: Dike or erosion first?
blocks.q: A dike cuts tilted layers but ends at an unconformity, where flat layers cover it. Which came first, the dike or the erosion?
steps: The dike's top is cut off at the erosion surface, so it was already there when erosion wore the rock down.
So the dike came first, then the erosion, then the flat layers.

blocks.html: It is tempting to list the layers from bottom to top and stop, forgetting the tilting, folding, faulting and erosion between them. Those are events too, often the most important ones. Check your list: does it explain why the lower layers are tilted and the upper ones are not? If not, an event is missing.

Relative dating puts events in order. To put numbers on them, geologists use radioactive atoms, which you met in Half-Life and Absolute Age and Radioactive Decay. A parent isotope decays into a daughter at a steady rate, and the decay can't be sped up or slowed down by heat, pressure or chemistry. That makes it a clock.

In each half-life, half of the remaining parent atoms decay. After $n$ half-lives the parent left is $P = P_0\left(\tfrac12\right)^n$, and every decayed atom became a daughter: $D = P_0 - P$. Divide: $\dfrac{D}{P} = 2^n - 1$, so $n = \log_2\left(1 + \dfrac{D}{P}\right)$ and the age is $t = t_{1/2}\log_2\left(1 + \dfrac{D}{P}\right)$ (an exponential equation solved with a log). This assumes the mineral held no daughter atoms when it formed and lost none since; zircon, which rejects lead as it crystallizes, is ideal for uranium–lead dating.

Daughter ÷ parent

blocks.html: Count half-lives from the daughter-to-parent ratio: 1 means one half-life, 3 means two, 7 means three. In general $t = t_{1/2}\log_2(1 + D/P)$. The clock starts when a mineral crystallizes and traps the parent.

blocks.name: es-halflife
blocks.cap: Uranium-235 atoms in a zircon decaying to lead-207. Step through half-lives and watch the daughter-to-parent ratio climb: 1, 3, 7, 15.

blocks.title: Whole half-lives
blocks.q: A zircon has 7 atoms of lead-207 for every atom of uranium-235 (half-life 704 million years). How old is it?
steps: $D/P = 7$ means $\tfrac18$ of the parent is left: 3 half-lives.
Age $= 3 \times 704 = 2,112$ million years, about 2.1 billion years.

blocks.title: Using the logarithm
blocks.q: A zircon has $D/P = 0.25$ for uranium-238 → lead-206 (half-life 4.47 billion years). How old is it?
steps: Age $= 0.322 \times 4,470 \approx 1,440$ million years.

blocks.html: Many people think carbon-14 dates dinosaur bones and ancient rocks. With a half-life of 5,730 years, carbon-14 works only for once-living material up to about 50,000 years old; after that too little is left to measure. Dinosaurs died out 66 million years ago, more than 11,000 carbon-14 half-lives. Their ages come from uranium–lead and potassium–argon dates on volcanic ash and lava above and below their fossils. Check: match the half-life to the age you expect.
Watch atoms decay one at a time in the Build an Atom lab, then come back and date a rock.

Radiometric dating works only if the clock fits the job. A clock must tick slowly enough that some parent remains, fast enough that daughter has built up, and it must have started at the event you want to date.

head: Clock
Half-life
Good for
Dates
rows: wood, bone, charcoal, shell: when the organism died
volcanic rock and ash: when it cooled and trapped argon
about 1 million years to Earth's age
blocks.cap: Common radioactive clocks (rounded).

blocks.html: After about 10 half-lives, only $\tfrac{1}{1,024}$ of the parent remains, too little to measure well: that sets the upper limit. Too few half-lives and too little daughter has formed: that sets the lower limit. And the clock must start at the event: an organism stops taking in carbon-14 when it dies; a crystal traps uranium and shuts out lead when it forms; a lava flow lets argon gas escape until it cools solid. (Potassium-40 also decays to calcium-40, which labs account for.) Using two uranium clocks in one zircon gives two independent ages that must agree, a built-in check.

Match the clock to the material and age: carbon-14 for remains up to about 50,000 years; potassium–argon for volcanic rock; uranium–lead in zircon for millions to billions of years. Sedimentary rock is dated by the igneous rocks around it.

blocks.name: es-halflife
blocks.cap: Pick an isotope and compare half-lives and useful age ranges.

blocks.title: Pick the clock
blocks.q: Which clock would date a layer of volcanic ash about 2 million years old?
steps: Carbon-14 is far too short-lived, and ash was never alive.
Potassium–argon (or uranium–lead in zircons from the ash) fits: volcanic material, millions of years old.

blocks.title: The carbon-14 limit
blocks.q: How many half-lives of carbon-14 pass in 50,000 years, and what fraction is left?
steps: $50,000 \div 5,730 \approx 8.7$ half-lives.
$\left(\tfrac12\right)^{8.7} \approx 0.0024$: about 0.24% remains, near the limit of measurement.

blocks.html: It seems natural to date a sandstone by dating its grains. But each grain is a piece of an older rock, and its clock started when that rock crystallized, perhaps a billion years before the sand was laid down. Sedimentary layers are dated indirectly, by the ash beds, lava flows and dikes above, below and through them. Check: ask when the clock in your sample started.
See isotopes and half-lives up close in the Build an Atom lab.

Most fossils lie in sedimentary rock, which can't be dated directly (its grains are older than the rock). So how do we know the dinosaurs died out 66 million years ago? By combining relative order with dated igneous rocks: ash beds, lava flows and dikes.

Each dated igneous rock gives a limit. A layer resting on an ash bed is younger than the ash. A layer covered by an ash bed is older than that ash. A layer cut by a dike is older than the dike. So a sedimentary layer between two dated beds is bracketed: it formed sometime between their ages. Sediment does not pile up at a steady, known rate, so the honest answer is a range, not a single number. More dated layers make the brackets tighter; today, ash beds near the end of the dinosaurs are dated to within tens of thousands of years.
A sedimentary layer is younger than any dated rock it rests on, and older than any dated rock that covers it or cuts it. Report its age as the range between those limits.

blocks.name: es-strata
blocks.cap: An ammonite-bearing shale between two dated ash beds, all cut by a dated dike.

blocks.title: Between two ash beds
blocks.q: A shale with ammonites lies on an ash bed dated 95 million years and under an ash bed dated 92 million years. How old is the shale?
steps: On the 95-million-year ash: younger than 95.
Under the 92-million-year ash: older than 92.
So it formed between 95 and 92 million years ago, and so did its ammonites.

blocks.title: Using a dike
blocks.q: A limestone rests on an ash bed dated 120 million years and is cut by a dike dated 101 million years. How old is the limestone?
steps: Younger than the ash below it: less than 120.
The dike cuts it, so it existed before 101.
Between 120 and 101 million years old.

blocks.html: It is tempting to give one age, often the average, when the evidence only brackets a range. A shale between ash beds of 95 and 92 million years could be anywhere in between, and its lower part is older than its upper part. Check what each dated rock actually tells you: one limit each.
With radiometric dates on the time line that began 4.54 billion years ago, we can place the great events of Earth's history. Most of the story happened before animals with skeletons even existed.

head: About this long ago
Event
rows: oldest known mineral grains (zircons): early crust and probably liquid water
oldest widely accepted fossils: stromatolites built by microbes
oxygen builds up in the air (the Great Oxidation Event)
the Cambrian explosion: animals with shells and skeletons spread
the five great mass extinctions; the largest at 252, the end of the dinosaurs at 66
blocks.cap: Major events, rounded (International Chronostratigraphic Chart and other sources).

blocks.html: How do we know the air once lacked oxygen? Rocks older than about 2.4 billion years contain river-worn grains of pyrite and uraninite, minerals that oxygen would quickly destroy; younger rocks contain red beds stained by iron oxide. Photosynthesizing microbes (cyanobacteria) slowly released the oxygen, changing the planet's chemistry. Mass extinctions show up as sudden losses of many fossil species at once, across the world, at the same dated layers.

Earth's air had almost no oxygen for its first two billion years; oxygen built up about 2.4 billion years ago. Animals with skeletons appeared about 539 million years ago, and five mass extinctions punctuate the record since.

blocks.name: es-deep-time
blocks.cap: Earth's history squeezed into 24 hours. Our species arrives in the last few seconds.

blocks.title: Before the animals
blocks.q: What fraction of Earth's history passed before the Cambrian explosion?
steps: $4,540 - 539 = 4,001$ million years passed first.
$4,001 \div 4,540 \approx 0.88$: about 88% of Earth's history.

blocks.title: On a 24-hour clock
blocks.q: If Earth's history were one day, how many minutes before midnight did the dinosaurs die out (66 million years ago)?
steps: Fraction still to come: $66 \div 4,540 = 0.0145$.
$0.0145 \times 1,440 \approx 21$ minutes before midnight.

blocks.html: It is easy to assume the air always had plenty of oxygen. For its first two billion years Earth's air had almost none; animals like us could not have breathed it. Check the rocks: grains of pyrite in ancient river sands could not survive in today's air.

sources.name: International Commission on Stratigraphy, International Chronostratigraphic Chart (rounded ages)

blocks.html: In the 1950s and 1960s, ships towing magnetometers back and forth across the oceans found something no one expected: the seafloor's magnetism runs in long stripes, alternately stronger and weaker, parallel to the mid-ocean ridges and mirrored on both sides. Paleomagnetism explains them, and they became the clinching evidence for seafloor spreading.

At a ridge crest, basalt erupts, cools and records the field of the moment. Then the plates move apart and that strip of new crust is split and carried away to both sides, while fresh lava fills the middle. When the field flips, the next crust records the opposite direction. So the seafloor becomes a tape recorder of reversals, playing out in both directions from the crest. Rocks on land had already given the dates of the reversals, so each stripe boundary has an age, and distance ÷ age gives the speed.

Magnetic stripes match the reversal time line, so distance from the crest ÷ age gives the half spreading rate: how fast each plate moves away from the ridge. The plates separate at the full rate, twice that. Conveniently, 1 km per million years = 1 mm per year.

blocks.name: es-boundary
blocks.cap: Spreading at a ridge. Run time forward and watch new stripes form at the crest and march outward on both sides.

blocks.title: Spreading rate from a stripe
blocks.q: The boundary of the most recent reversal, 0.77 million years old, lies 19.3 km from the crest. What is the half spreading rate?
steps: Rate $= \dfrac{19.3\,\text{km}}{0.77\,\text{million years}} \approx 25\,\text{km per million years}$.
$1\,\text{km}$ per million years is $10^6\,\text{mm} \div 10^6\,\text{yr} = 1\,\text{mm/yr}$, so the half rate is about $25\,\text{mm/yr}$.
The full rate, the speed at which the plates separate, is about $50\,\text{mm/yr}$.

blocks.title: How old is the seafloor?
blocks.q: A ridge spreads at a half rate of 30 mm/yr. How old is the seafloor 600 km from the crest?
steps: 30 mm/yr is 30 km per million years.
$600 \div 30 = 20$ million years.

blocks.html: Half and full spreading rates are easy to mix up. The half rate is how fast one plate moves away from the ridge; the two plates move apart at twice that. Check which you have: a stripe's distance from the crest gives the half rate; the distance between the matching stripes on both sides gives the full rate.

sources.name: USGS, This Dynamic Earth: The Story of Plate Tectonics (Kious and Tilling)

blocks.html: Plates move a few centimeters a year, about as fast as fingernails grow. Magnetic stripes give average rates over millions of years. Today, GPS stations bolted to bedrock measure plate motion directly, to a fraction of a millimeter per year, every day.

A GPS station's velocity is an arrow (a vector) with an east part and a north part, measured against a fixed global frame. That frame is a convenience; what matters at a plate boundary is how one side moves relative to the other. Relative velocity is a subtraction, done part by part: $\vec v_{B \text{ rel } A} = (v_{E,B} - v_{E,A},\; v_{N,B} - v_{N,A})$. Its size comes from the Pythagorean theorem, $\sqrt{v_E^2 + v_N^2}$. And whether the boundary opens or closes depends on whether the relative velocity points away from or toward the other station.

A GPS velocity has east and north parts. Subtract one station's velocity from the other's to get relative motion; use Pythagoras for its speed, and its direction along the line between them to see whether the gap opens or closes.

blocks.name: es-plates
blocks.cap: GPS stations on both sides of a fault. Pick a pair and compare their arrows with their difference (dashed).

blocks.title: A station's speed
blocks.q: A station moves 21 mm/yr east and 20 mm/yr north. How fast is it moving?

blocks.title: Opening or closing?
blocks.q: Station B is 100 km east of station A. A moves 10 mm/yr east and 5 mm/yr north; B moves 30 mm/yr east and 20 mm/yr north. How does B move relative to A?
steps: East: $30 - 10 = 20\,\text{mm/yr}$. North: $20 - 5 = 15\,\text{mm/yr}$.
Relative speed: $\sqrt{20^2 + 15^2} = 25\,\text{mm/yr}$.
B lies east of A and moves 20 mm/yr farther east, so the gap opens by 20 mm/yr; the 15 mm/yr north part slides B sideways past A.

blocks.html: It is natural to read each station's arrow as its motion relative to its neighbor. Two stations with big arrows pointing the same way might hardly be moving relative to each other at all. Check by subtracting: only the difference shows what the boundary between them is doing.

sources.name: USGS, This Dynamic Earth: The Story of Plate Tectonics (Kious and Tilling)

blocks.html: What moves the plates? Convection in the mantle is part of the answer, but the plates are not simply rafts on a moving current. The spreading rates of the different plates point to what pulls hardest.

New ocean lithosphere is hot. As it moves away from the ridge it cools from above, thickens, contracts and grows denser, so it also sinks lower: young seafloor is about 2,500 m deep, and its depth grows roughly as $d \approx 2,500 + 350\sqrt{t}$ meters ($t$ in million years). After a few tens of millions of years the plate is denser than the hot mantle beneath it. Where it bends down at a trench, the sinking edge (the slab) drags the rest of the plate after it: slab pull. Meanwhile, the plate slides gently downhill away from the high, hot ridge: ridge push.

Plates are driven mainly by gravity: cold, dense slabs sinking at subduction zones pull hardest (slab pull), and plates slide off high ridges (ridge push). Plates with long sinking edges move fastest.

blocks.name: es-boundary
blocks.cap: The forces on a plate: slab pull at the trench, ridge push at the ridge.

blocks.title: How deep is old seafloor?
blocks.q: Using $d \approx 2,500 + 350\sqrt{t}$, how deep is 49-million-year-old seafloor, and how much deeper than the ridge crest?
steps: The crest is at 2,500 m, so the old floor is 2,450 m deeper: a long, gentle slope the plate slides down.

blocks.title: The evidence
blocks.q: The Pacific plate, edged by trenches, moves 5 to 10 cm/yr; the Eurasian plate, with almost no sinking edge, moves 1 to 2 cm/yr. What does that suggest?
steps: If mantle currents simply carried plates, speed would not depend on whether a plate has a sinking edge.
Instead, plates with long subducting edges are fastest: the sinking slab is pulling.
blocks.a: Slab pull is the main driving force.

blocks.html: The picture of plates as rafts carried along by mantle currents is popular but misleading. The plates are the cold top of the mantle's own convection, and their sinking edges are what drive the flow. Check with speeds: if rafting were the rule, big continents would move as fast as ocean plates.

sources.name: USGS, This Dynamic Earth: The Story of Plate Tectonics (Kious and Tilling)

blocks.html: Where an ocean plate meets another plate head-on, the denser one sinks into the mantle at a subduction zone. Subduction zones make the deepest trenches, the largest earthquakes and chains of explosive volcanoes, all from the same sinking slab.

Old ocean lithosphere is cold and dense (oceanic crust about $3.0\,\text{g/cm}^3$, continental about $2.7$), so it sinks beneath a continent or younger ocean plate. As the slab descends it stays cold and brittle, so it breaks in earthquakes far deeper than anywhere else, down to about 700 km. Plotted on a cross-section, those earthquakes trace the slab: a Wadati–Benioff zone. At about 100 km depth, heat and pressure drive water out of the slab's minerals. The water rises into the hot mantle wedge above and lowers its melting point: flux melting. The magma rises to build a volcanic arc.

At a subduction zone the denser plate sinks; earthquakes trace the slab hundreds of kilometers down, and water released at about 100 km melts the mantle above it to feed arc volcanoes. The slab's dip sets how far inland the volcanoes stand: distance $= 100\,\text{km} \div \tan(\text{dip})$.

blocks.name: es-boundary
blocks.cap: An ocean plate sinking beneath a continent: earthquakes (dots) along the slab, and melting (orange) in the wedge above it.

blocks.title: Slab dip from earthquakes
blocks.q: Earthquakes 150 km deep lie 200 km inland from the trench. What is the slab's dip?
steps: Dip $= \tan^{-1}(0.75) \approx 37^\circ$.

blocks.title: Where are the volcanoes?
blocks.q: A slab dips $30^\circ$. Where do arc volcanoes form?
steps: Above the point where the slab is about 100 km deep.
Distance $= \dfrac{100}{\tan 30^\circ} = \dfrac{100}{0.577} \approx 173\,\text{km}$ from the trench.
A gentler slab puts its volcanoes farther inland; a steeper one brings them closer to the trench.

blocks.html: It is natural to think the sinking plate melts to make the arc's magma. Mostly it doesn't: the slab is cold and stays solid. The water it gives off lowers the melting point of the mantle above it, and that mantle melts. Check with temperatures: the slab is hundreds of degrees cooler than the mantle around it, which is why it can still break in earthquakes at 600 km.

sources.name: USGS, This Dynamic Earth: The Story of Plate Tectonics (Kious and Tilling)

blocks.html: Ocean plates sink; continents don't. When subduction swallows the ocean between two continents, they collide. And when a continent is pulled apart, it floats lower and splits. Buoyancy explains both.

Continental crust is about $2.7\,\text{g/cm}^3$, far lighter than the mantle ($3.3$). It can be dragged down a short way, but it bobs back up, so a collision crumples and stacks the crust instead. Shortening a belt of crust thickens it (in cross-section, width × thickness stays the same), and thick crust floats high, with a deep root: the Himalayas and the Tibetan Plateau rest on crust about 70 km thick, double the normal. Stretch a continent instead and the crust thins; thin crust sinks, faults drop long blocks, and hot mantle rises and melts, building a rift valley. Stretch far enough and the continent splits and the sea floods in.

Continental crust is too buoyant to subduct, so collisions thicken it into high mountains with deep roots (only about 18% of the extra thickness shows as height). Stretching thins it into rift valleys and, eventually, new oceans.

blocks.name: es-boundary
blocks.cap: A continent–continent collision. Switch to the rift view to see the opposite: a continent pulled apart.

blocks.title: Doubling the crust
blocks.q: A belt of crust 400 km wide and 35 km thick is squeezed to 200 km wide. How thick does it become?
steps: Width × thickness stays the same: $400 \times 35 = 200 \times H$.
$H = 70\,\text{km}$, as under Tibet.

blocks.title: How high does it float?
blocks.q: The crust thickens by 35 km. With crust $2.7$ and mantle $3.3$, how much higher does the surface stand?
steps: The extra thickness splits into height $h$ and root $4.5h$: $h + 4.5h = 35$.
$5.5h = 35$, so $h \approx 6.4\,\text{km}$; in reality erosion and weaker crust keep Tibet at about 5 km.

blocks.html: It is tempting to expect continents to subduct like ocean floor. They are too light to sink far, which is why collisions build the highest mountains instead of trenches. Check with fossils: marine limestone at the top of Everest is old seafloor scraped up between India and Asia, not continent that sank and came back.

sources.name: USGS, This Dynamic Earth: The Story of Plate Tectonics (Kious and Tilling)

blocks.html: Mid-ocean ridges are not continuous lines; they are broken into segments, offset by transform faults, a kind of strike-slip fault that is also a plate boundary. Along them, plates slide past each other, neither making nor destroying crust.

Picture two ridge segments offset by 100 km, joined by a transform fault. Each segment spreads, carrying seafloor away from it on both sides. On the stretch of fault between the segments, the two sides belong to different plates moving in opposite directions: that part is active and full of earthquakes. Beyond the segments, the fault's scar (a fracture zone) continues, but both sides belong to the same plate and move together: no slip. And here is the surprise: the sense of slip on the active part comes from spreading, not from the offset. The ridge segments never move apart; the offset can stay the same for millions of years.

Transform faults offset ridge segments and let plates slide past each other. Only the part between the segments is active; the slip there runs opposite to what the offset suggests, at the full spreading rate.

blocks.name: es-boundary
blocks.cap: Two ridge segments joined by a transform fault. Watch which stretch has motion on both sides in opposite directions.

blocks.title: Which way does it slip?
blocks.q: A north–south ridge spreads east–west. Its northern segment is offset 80 km west of its southern segment. Standing on the south side of the active transform and looking north, which way does the far side move?
steps: Between the segments, the north side lies east of the northern segment, on the east-moving plate.
The south side lies west of the southern segment, on the west-moving plate.
Looking north, the far side moves east, to your right: right-lateral. The offset (north segment shifted west) would wrongly suggest left-lateral.

blocks.title: How fast?
blocks.q: A ridge spreads at a half rate of 20 mm/yr. How fast do the sides of its active transform slide past each other?
steps: Each side moves 20 mm/yr away from its own segment, in opposite directions.
$2 \times 20 = 40\,\text{mm/yr}$, the full rate.

blocks.html: A natural reading of an offset ridge is that a fault dragged the ridge apart, so the slip must match the offset. It doesn't: on the active transform the plates move in the opposite sense to the offset. Check by asking which plate each side belongs to and which way that plate spreads.

sources.name: USGS, This Dynamic Earth: The Story of Plate Tectonics (Kious and Tilling)

blocks.html: In the 1960s, J. Tuzo Wilson noticed that old mountain belts mark where ancient oceans once closed, and that oceans open where continents split. Put rifts and collisions on a time line and oceans have a life story: the Wilson cycle.

head: Stage
What happens
Example today
rows: a narrow sea floods the rift; a new ridge forms
the ocean grows at a ridge; its edges are quiet
old, dense seafloor starts sinking at its edges
the ocean shrinks as continents approach
continents meet and build mountains along a suture
blocks.cap: The stages of the Wilson cycle.

blocks.html: The cycle runs on density. Rifts open where a continent is stretched over hot mantle; the ocean widens as long as its ridge spreads. As the seafloor ages it cools, grows dense, and eventually begins to sink at subduction zones, so the ocean starts to close. When the continents meet, their buoyant crust stops subduction and piles up into mountains, welding the pieces into a larger continent, sometimes a supercontinent, which may later rift again. One full cycle takes very roughly 300 to 500 million years.
Oceans open and close in a cycle: rift, young ocean, wide ocean, subduction, closing, collision. Supercontinents form when the continents gather, and Pangaea was only the most recent of several.

blocks.name: es-plates
blocks.cap: Run time from 250 million years ago to today and watch Pangaea split and the Atlantic open.

blocks.title: Opening an ocean
blocks.q: How long does it take to open an ocean 4,500 km wide at a full spreading rate of 25 mm/yr?
steps: 25 mm/yr is 25 km per million years.
$4,500 \div 25 = 180$ million years, about the age of the Atlantic.

blocks.title: Name the stage
blocks.q: What stage is the Red Sea in?
steps: Arabia split from Africa, and new ocean floor now forms along the middle of the sea.
A narrow sea with a young ridge: stage 2, a young ocean.

blocks.html: It is common to think Pangaea was Earth's first and only supercontinent. Ancient mountain belts record earlier ones: Rodinia came together about a billion years ago and began breaking up around 750 million years ago, and an older one, Columbia (or Nuna), may date from about 1.8 billion years ago. Check the time: Pangaea formed only about 300 million years ago, in the last 7% of Earth's history.

sources.name: USGS, This Dynamic Earth: The Story of Plate Tectonics (Kious and Tilling)

blocks.html: After the 1906 San Francisco earthquake, surveyors found that fences and roads crossing the San Andreas Fault had been offset by up to about 6 m. Harry Fielding Reid used the survey data to explain why: the rock had been bending for decades and then snapped back. His elastic rebound theory connects faults to earthquakes.

Plates move steadily, millimeters a year, but friction locks the fault. So the rock on both sides bends, storing strain like a bent stick or a stretched spring. When the stress exceeds the friction, the fault slips in seconds, the bent rock springs back, and the stored energy leaves as seismic waves. Then the locking starts again. Over many cycles, the fault's average slip must keep up with the plates: if each big earthquake slips $D$ meters and the plates move $v$ per year, the average time between quakes is $T = \dfrac{D}{v}$.
A locked fault bends and stores strain, then snaps back in an earthquake. Average time between large quakes = slip per quake ÷ slip rate. It is an average, not a schedule.

blocks.name: es-structures
blocks.cap: A fence across a locked fault. Run the years forward: the fence bends, then the fault slips and it snaps back, offset.

blocks.title: Time between quakes
blocks.q: A fault slips 35 mm/yr on average, and each large earthquake slips about 4 m. How often, on average, do large quakes happen?
steps: $4,000 \div 35 \approx 114$ years, on average.

blocks.title: Small quakes can't keep up
blocks.q: About how many magnitude 5 earthquakes release the energy of one magnitude 7?
steps: Each step of 1 in magnitude means about $10^{1.5} \approx 32$ times more energy.
A fault storing strain for a magnitude 7 would need a thousand magnitude 5 quakes to release it.

blocks.html: It is comforting to think that many small earthquakes let off the pressure and prevent a big one. They release far too little energy: it takes about 1,000 magnitude 5 quakes to match one magnitude 7. Check with the numbers before trusting the comfort.

sources.name: USGS Earthquake Hazards Program, Earthquake Magnitude, Energy Release, and Shaking Intensity
USGS, This Dynamic Earth: The Story of Plate Tectonics (Kious and Tilling)

blocks.html: When an earthquake strikes, seismographs around the world record it within minutes. The first question is where it was. In Earthquakes and Seismic Waves you saw P waves outrun S waves. That race is the key, and solving a formula for one letter turns it into a distance.

Both waves leave the focus at the same instant and travel the same distance $d$, but at different speeds. The S wave arrives later by $\Delta t = \dfrac{d}{v_S} - \dfrac{d}{v_P}$. Factor out $d$ and solve: $d = \Delta t \cdot \dfrac{v_P v_S}{v_P - v_S}$. With typical crustal speeds $v_P \approx 6\,\text{km/s}$ and $v_S \approx 3.5\,\text{km/s}$, the fraction is $\dfrac{6 \times 3.5}{2.5} = 8.4$: each second of S−P gap means about 8.4 km of distance. Seismologists use travel-time curves built from thousands of earthquakes, because real speeds change with depth, but the idea is the same.

The gap between P and S arrivals grows with distance: $d = \Delta t \cdot \dfrac{v_P v_S}{v_P - v_S}$, about 8.4 km per second of gap for crustal speeds. Once you know $d$, you can find when the quake began.

blocks.name: es-seismic
blocks.cap: Seismograms at three distances, and the travel-time curves. Slide a gap along the curves and read the distance.

blocks.title: Distance from the gap
blocks.q: At a station, S waves arrive 20 s after P waves. How far away was the earthquake ($v_P = 6$, $v_S = 3.5\,\text{km/s}$)?
steps: Check: P takes $168 \div 6 = 28\,\text{s}$; S takes $168 \div 3.5 = 48\,\text{s}$; the gap is $20\,\text{s}$.

blocks.title: When did it start?
blocks.q: For that station, the P wave arrived at 10:42:30. When did the earthquake begin?
steps: P travel time: $168 \div 6 = 28\,\text{s}$.

blocks.html: The same race works with a thunderstorm: the flash arrives almost at once and the sound follows at about 343 m/s, so each second between flash and thunder means about a third of a kilometer.

It seems as if one arrival time should give the distance: distance = speed × time. But the time in that formula is travel time, and nobody knew when the earthquake began. Check by asking what you know: the arrival clock time, not the travel time. The gap between two arrivals needs no start time.

sources.name: USGS Earthquake Hazards Program, Earthquake Magnitude, Energy Release, and Shaking Intensity

blocks.html: The S−P gap tells one station how far away an earthquake was, but not in which direction. All it knows is that the epicenter (the point on the surface above the focus) lies somewhere on a circle around the station. With the distance formula, three circles pin it down.

Two circles usually cross at two points, so two stations leave two possible epicenters. The two points are mirror images across the line joining the stations. A third station's circle passes through only one of them, and that is the epicenter. To check a candidate point by hand, compute its distance to the third station with $d = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2}$ and compare it with that station's measured distance. Real networks use dozens of stations and solve for depth and start time too, but this is the core idea, called trilateration (GPS works the same way).
Each station gives a circle of the right distance. Two circles cross at two points; the third circle picks the one that is the epicenter.

blocks.name: es-seismic
blocks.cap: Draw the circles one at a time: one gives a ring, two give two crossing points, three pick the epicenter.

blocks.title: Pick the right point
blocks.q: Station 3 is at $(100, 40)$ on a grid in km and is 50 km from the quake. The circles of stations 1 and 2 cross at $P(60, 10)$ and $Q(-20, 70)$. Which is the epicenter?
steps: Distance from station 3 to $P$: $\sqrt{(60 - 100)^2 + (10 - 40)^2} = \sqrt{1,600 + 900} = 50\,\text{km}$. It matches.
Distance to $Q$: $\sqrt{(-120)^2 + 30^2} \approx 124\,\text{km}$. It doesn't.
So the epicenter is $P(60, 10)$.

blocks.title: From gaps to circles
blocks.q: Three stations record S−P gaps of 10, 15 and 20 s. What are the radii of their circles (8.4 km per second)?
steps: The station with the shortest gap is closest to the quake.

blocks.html: It is easy to think two stations are enough. Two circles usually cross at two points, and both fit the two stations equally well. Check by sketching: the third circle is what breaks the tie.

blocks.html: In Earthquake Magnitude you learned that each step on the magnitude scale means much stronger shaking. Seismologists today use moment magnitude, $M_w$, because it measures the earthquake at its source, the fault slip itself, and it keeps working for the largest quakes. It runs on logarithms.

The size of an earthquake is how much rock broke and how far it moved. Seismic moment captures that: $M_0 = \mu A D$, where $A$ is the area of fault that slipped, $D$ the average slip, and $\mu \approx 3 \times 10^{10}\,\text{Pa}$ the rock's stiffness, giving newton-meters. Moments range over many powers of ten, so the magnitude takes a log: $M_w = \tfrac{2}{3}(\log_{10} M_0 - 9.1)$. Because of the $\tfrac23$, multiplying $M_0$ by 1,000 adds 2 to the magnitude, and each step of 1 means about $10^{1.5} \approx 32$ times more energy (and seismic waves about 10 times larger).
$M_w = \tfrac{2}{3}(\log_{10} M_0 - 9.1)$ with $M_0 = \mu A D$. Each magnitude step means about 32 times more energy; two steps mean about 1,000 times.

blocks.name: es-seismic
blocks.cap: Compare two earthquakes' waves and energy, and build a magnitude from a fault's area and slip.

blocks.title: Magnitude from a fault
blocks.q: A fault ruptures over an area 100 km long and 20 km deep, with 2 m of average slip ($\mu = 3 \times 10^{10}\,\text{Pa}$). What is $M_w$?

blocks.title: Energy ratio
blocks.q: How much more energy does a magnitude 8 release than a magnitude 6?

blocks.html: The original Richter scale (1935) used the height of waves on one kind of seismograph. For very large earthquakes those waves stop growing, so the old scale saturates near magnitude 7 to 8. Moment magnitude is built from the fault itself, so it keeps working for the largest quakes.

Many people think magnitude 10 is the top of a 1-to-10 scale. The scale has no top: magnitude grows with fault area times slip. But size is limited by real faults. The largest recorded earthquake, Chile 1960, was about $M_w$ 9.5, on a rupture roughly 1,000 km long; a magnitude 10 would need a rupture far longer than any known fault. Check with $M_0 = \mu A D$: what area would it take?

blocks.html: Magnitude measures an earthquake at its source: one number per quake. People, though, feel shaking where they are, and that varies from place to place. Intensity describes the shaking at a location, on the Modified Mercalli Intensity scale, from I (not felt) to XII (near-total destruction), written in Roman numerals.

head: Intensity
What happens (abbreviated)
rows: noticed by only a few people at rest
noticed indoors by many; dishes and windows rattle
felt by everyone; some furniture moves; slight damage
considerable damage to ordinary buildings; chimneys and walls fall
most masonry and frame buildings destroyed
blocks.cap: Selected Modified Mercalli intensities (paraphrased from USGS).

blocks.html: Shaking depends on more than magnitude. Waves spread out and lose energy with distance, so shaking fades away from the epicenter. A shallow quake shakes the surface harder than a deep one. And the ground matters: waves slow down and grow taller entering soft sediment, which can slosh like jelly, and waterlogged sand can lose its strength and flow (liquefaction). Building design matters too. USGS maps of shaking combine instrument recordings with thousands of "Did You Feel It?" reports from the public.
An earthquake has one magnitude but many intensities. Intensity is highest near the epicenter, for shallow quakes, and on soft, wet ground.

blocks.name: es-seismic
blocks.cap: Shaking intensity around an epicenter. Turn the soft-sediment basin on and off.

blocks.title: Near or far
blocks.q: A magnitude 6.5 quake strikes. Town A, on bedrock, is 15 km away; town B, also on bedrock, is 90 km away. Which shakes harder?
steps: Same earthquake, same ground: distance decides.
Town A, closer to the source, has the higher intensity.

blocks.title: Soft ground
blocks.q: In 1985 a magnitude 8 earthquake struck about 350 km from Mexico City, yet the city suffered terrible damage. Why?
steps: Much of the city sits on soft sediment of an old lake bed.
The sediment amplified the shaking, especially for buildings of certain heights, raising the intensity far above that of nearby areas on firmer ground.
blocks.a: Soft lake-bed sediment amplified the shaking.

blocks.html: It is natural to think an earthquake has a single intensity, the way it has one magnitude. Intensity is different at every place. Check the words: magnitude is about the quake; intensity is about where you are.

blocks.html: Nobody can predict the day of the next big earthquake. What scientists can do is estimate chances, using slip rates, records of past quakes and compound probability. A forecast such as "a 72% chance of a magnitude 6.7 or larger in the San Francisco Bay Area within 30 years" comes from this kind of reasoning.

Suppose the chance of a large quake in any one year is $p$, independent from year to year. The chance of no quake in a year is $1 - p$. For $n$ quiet years in a row, multiply: $(1 - p)^n$ (an exponential function). So the chance of at least one is $P = 1 - (1 - p)^n$. You can't simply add yearly chances: adding counts the years with two or more quakes twice, and for long spans it can even pass 100%. (Real forecasts also let $p$ grow as strain builds, but the "at least one" logic is the same.)
Chance of at least one event in $n$ years: $1 - (1 - p)^n$, where $p$ is the yearly chance. For a recurrence interval $T$, $p \approx \tfrac{1}{T}$.

blocks.name: es-chance
blocks.cap: Simulate many 30-year stretches with a 2% yearly chance and count how many have at least one event.

blocks.title: Two percent a year
blocks.q: A fault has a 2% chance of a large quake each year. What is the chance of at least one in 30 years?
steps: No quake in a year: $0.98$.
No quake in 30 years: $0.98^{30} \approx 0.545$.
At least one: $1 - 0.545 = 0.455$, about 45%, not 60%.

blocks.title: From a forecast back to a year
blocks.q: A 30-year forecast gives a 50% chance. What yearly chance does that mean?
steps: $p \approx 0.0228$, about 2.3% per year.

blocks.html: Adding the yearly chances is the most common slip: 2% a year for 30 years seems like 60%. The chance of at least one is $1 - 0.98^{30} \approx 45\%$. Check with an extreme: 5% a year for 30 years would "add" to 150%, which is impossible.

blocks.html: When a subduction zone earthquake jolts the seafloor up or down by meters, it lifts or drops the whole column of water above it, from the bottom to the surface. That water spreads out as a tsunami, a series of waves unlike any wind wave.

Wind waves stir only the top few meters of the sea and are tens of meters long. A tsunami moves the whole depth and can be hundreds of kilometers long, much longer than the ocean is deep. For such waves the speed depends only on depth: $v = \sqrt{g d}$. In the open ocean, 4,000 m deep, that is about 200 m/s (over 700 km/h), yet the wave may be less than a meter high, unnoticed by ships. Near shore the depth shrinks, the front slows, and the water behind catches up and piles up, so the wave grows tall. Because the waves are so long, each one floods inland for many minutes, like a fast-rising tide, and several arrive in a series.
A tsunami is a series of very long waves from a sudden shift of the seafloor. It travels at $v = \sqrt{g d}$: as fast as a jet airliner in the deep ocean, slowing and growing taller near shore.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: Tsunami speed (up, in km/h) against ocean depth (across, in km), from $v = \sqrt{gd}$. Drag the point from the deep ocean toward the shore and watch the wave slow down.

blocks.title: Speed in the open ocean
blocks.q: How fast does a tsunami cross ocean 4,000 m deep?
steps: $v = \sqrt{9.8 \times 4,000} = \sqrt{39,200} \approx 198\,\text{m/s}$.
$198 \times 3.6 \approx 713\,\text{km/h}$.

blocks.title: Crossing the Pacific
blocks.q: About how long does a tsunami take to cross 8,000 km of ocean averaging 4,000 m deep?
steps: About 11 hours. Warning centers use such travel times to alert coasts on the far side of the ocean.

blocks.html: A tsunami is often pictured as one giant breaking wave, like surf in a movie. It is usually a series of long waves that surge far inland, and the first is often not the largest; later waves can arrive many minutes apart. Check with the wavelength: with crests hundreds of kilometers apart, each wave takes many minutes to pass.

blocks.html: Landslides, rockfalls, slumps and creeping soil are all mass wasting: rock and soil moving downhill under gravity, with no river or glacier carrying them. In Erosion and Deposition gravity was in the background; here it is the whole story, and right-triangle trigonometry tells us when a slope gives way.

Picture a block of soil on a slope at angle $\theta$. Its weight $W$ splits into two parts: one pulling it down the slope, $W\sin\theta$, and one pressing it into the slope, $W\cos\theta$. Friction resists sliding, and it grows with the pressing force: friction $= W\cos\theta \tan\varphi$, where $\varphi$ is the material's friction angle (the steepest angle it can rest at). The factor of safety compares them: $FS = \dfrac{\text{resisting}}{\text{driving}} = \dfrac{W\cos\theta\tan\varphi}{W\sin\theta} = \dfrac{\tan\varphi}{\tan\theta}$ for dry, loose material. Above 1 the slope holds; below 1 it fails. Steepen the slope and the pull grows while the friction shrinks.

A slope fails when the downhill pull beats the friction and strength holding it: $FS = \dfrac{\tan\varphi}{\tan\theta}$ for dry, loose material, with failure below 1. Water filling the pores lowers the friction and can cut FS roughly in half.

blocks.name: es-landscape
blocks.cap: A slope with its forces. Steepen it, or soak it with water, and watch the factor of safety fall.

blocks.title: Is it stable?
blocks.q: Dry gravel with a friction angle of $35^\circ$ sits on a $30^\circ$ slope. Find FS.
steps: $FS = \dfrac{\tan 35^\circ}{\tan 30^\circ} = \dfrac{0.700}{0.577} \approx 1.21$.
Above 1: stable, but without much margin.

blocks.title: After heavy rain
blocks.q: The same slope becomes soaked, with water seeping down parallel to the surface. Then $FS \approx \dfrac{\gamma_{sat} - \gamma_w}{\gamma_{sat}}\cdot\dfrac{\tan\varphi}{\tan\theta}$, with soaked soil $20\,\text{kN/m}^3$ and water $9.8\,\text{kN/m}^3$. Find FS.
steps: $FS \approx 0.51 \times 1.21 \approx 0.62$. Below 1: the slope fails.

blocks.html: It is natural to think water makes slopes fail mainly by adding weight. The weight adds a little, but the bigger effect is that water under pressure in the pores pushes the grains apart, so they press together less and friction drops. Check with the formula: the water term reduces the friction part, not the pull.

Rivers do more work shaping the land than any other agent. Two numbers describe a stream: how steep it is and how much water it carries. In Landforms Made by Water you met valleys and floodplains; here we measure the water that makes them, keeping careful track of units.

Gradient is the drop in elevation per distance along the channel, often in meters per kilometer: steep near the source, gentle near the mouth. Discharge is the volume of water passing a point each second. Think of the water crossing a gauging line in one second: it fills a box as wide as the channel ($w$), as deep as the water ($d$), and as long as the distance the water travels in that second ($v$). So $Q = w \times d \times v$, in cubic meters per second. Discharge grows downstream as tributaries join.
Gradient = drop ÷ distance. Discharge $Q = w \times d \times v$ (cross-section area × average speed), in m³/s.

blocks.name: es-landscape
blocks.cap: A gauging station on a river. Change the width, depth and speed and watch the discharge.

blocks.title: Discharge at a gauge
blocks.q: A river is 25 m wide and 2 m deep on average, flowing 1.2 m/s. Find its discharge.
steps: Area: $25 \times 2 = 50\,\text{m}^2$.
$Q = 50 \times 1.2 = 60\,\text{m}^3/\text{s}$, enough to fill an Olympic pool in under a minute.

blocks.title: Gradient
blocks.q: A mountain stream drops 90 m in 3 km. A large river drops 30 m in 100 km. Compare their gradients.
steps: Stream: $90 \div 3 = 30\,\text{m/km}$.
River: $30 \div 100 = 0.3\,\text{m/km}$, a hundred times gentler.

blocks.html: USGS gauging stations measure thousands of U.S. rivers around the clock. They record the water level (the stage) and turn it into discharge with a rating curve, built from many hands-on measurements of width, depth and speed.

blocks.name: es-topo
blocks.cap: Contour lines bend upstream where they cross a stream; closely spaced contours along the channel mean a steep gradient.

blocks.html: A steep, foaming mountain stream looks faster and mightier than a big, calm river downstream. In fact the river usually carries far more water, and its average speed is often as high or higher: the stream loses much of its energy to friction against boulders in a shallow, rough bed. Check with $Q = wdv$: a wide, deep channel wins easily.
