blocks.html: Seen from the air, a lowland river loops back and forth across a broad, flat floodplain. Those loops, meanders, are not fixed; they grow and move. Flowing water and sediment transport explain the whole landscape.

Water flowing around a bend keeps its momentum and is flung toward the outside of the curve, where it runs deepest and fastest. Fast water erodes the outer bank into a steep cut bank; on the inside, slow water drops sand in a gentle point bar. So each bend eats outward and builds inward, and the meanders swing sideways across the valley. When two bends nearly meet, a flood can cut through the narrow neck; the abandoned loop becomes an oxbow lake. Floods spill over the banks, slow down and drop silt, building the floodplain. And a river can only erode down to its base level: sea level overall, or a lake or reservoir locally.

In a meander, the fastest water is on the outside of the bend, eroding a cut bank; the inside builds a point bar. Rivers cut down toward base level; raise base level and they deposit, lower it and they cut down.

blocks.name: es-landscape
blocks.cap: Run time forward: the meander grows by eroding outside and building inside, until the neck is cut and an oxbow lake is left.

blocks.title: How winding?
blocks.q: A river's channel is 36 km long between two towns 20 km apart along the valley. What is its sinuosity?
steps: Sinuosity = channel length ÷ valley length $= 36 \div 20 = 1.8$.
Above about 1.5, a river is called meandering.

blocks.title: A dam
blocks.q: A dam is built across a river. What happens upstream, and why?
steps: The reservoir is a new, higher local base level.
Where the river enters it, the water slows and drops its sediment, slowly filling the reservoir.
blocks.a: The river deposits sediment and fills the reservoir.

blocks.html: A common guess is that the water on the inside of a bend is fastest, because that path is shorter. It is on the outside. Check the banks: the outside bank is the steep, eroding one, and the inside is the sandy bar where you can wade.

"A 100-year flood" is one of the most misunderstood phrases in science. It does not mean a flood that comes once a century. It is a statement about chance: how often a river overflows its banks onto the floodplain it built, estimated from its record of discharge and the same probability as earthquake forecasts.

Take the largest flow of each year for $n$ years and rank them, the biggest as $m = 1$. The recurrence interval of the flood ranked $m$ is estimated as $T = \dfrac{n + 1}{m}$: over a long record, a flood that big or bigger is matched or exceeded on average once in $T$ years. That makes its chance in any single year $p = \tfrac{1}{T}$. So a 100-year flood has a 1% chance every year, including the year after one happens. Over $n$ years, the chance of at least one is $1 - (1 - p)^n$: over a 30-year mortgage, about 26% for a 100-year flood.
Recurrence interval $T = \dfrac{n + 1}{m}$ from ranked yearly peaks; yearly chance $= \tfrac{1}{T}$. A 100-year flood has a 1% chance every year.

blocks.name: es-chance
blocks.cap: A made-up river's yearly peak flows. Pick a flow and read its rank, recurrence interval and yearly chance.

blocks.title: Rank a record
blocks.q: A town's records give 9 years of yearly peak flows. The second largest was 720 m³/s. What is its recurrence interval?
steps: So a flow that large has about a 20% chance in any year. (A 9-year record is short; long records give better estimates.)

blocks.title: Over a mortgage
blocks.q: What is the chance of at least one 100-year flood in 30 years?
steps: No such flood in a year: $0.99$.
None in 30 years: $0.99^{30} \approx 0.74$.
At least one: $1 - 0.74 = 0.26$, about 26%, as the USGS points out.

blocks.html: Many people think that after a 100-year flood, the next one is 100 years away. The river has no memory: the chance is 1% every year, and two can come in back-to-back years. Check the definition: 1 in 100 is a chance per year, not a schedule.

blocks.html: In Groundwater and Aquifers you learned that most groundwater sits in the pore spaces of sand, gravel and cracked rock. It is not still: it flows, slowly, from where the water table is high toward where it is low. In 1856 Henry Darcy measured that flow through sand filters in Dijon, France, and found a simple law, a formula still used for every well and aquifer.

Water flows from high hydraulic head to low head; head is the height the water would rise to in a well. The steeper the head drops along the flow path, the faster it flows, just as a ball rolls faster down a steeper ramp. The steepness is the hydraulic gradient, $i = \dfrac{\Delta h}{L}$. How easily water passes through depends on the material: its hydraulic conductivity $K$ is large for gravel, small for clay. Darcy's law: $Q = K A \dfrac{\Delta h}{L}$, the volume per time through area $A$. The water itself squeezes through pores that are only a fraction $n$ (the porosity) of the rock, so it actually moves at $v = \dfrac{K i}{n}$.
Groundwater flows from high head to low head. Darcy's law: $Q = K A \dfrac{\Delta h}{L}$. Its actual speed, $\dfrac{K i}{n}$, is often less than a meter a day.

blocks.name: es-water
blocks.cap: Two wells in an aquifer. Pump well A and watch the water table dip toward it and the flow between the wells change.

blocks.title: Darcy's law
blocks.q: A sand aquifer has $K = 10\,\text{m/day}$. Across a section of $500\,\text{m}^2$, the head drops 4 m over 400 m. How much water flows through each day?
steps: Gradient: $4 \div 400 = 0.01$.
$Q = 10 \times 500 \times 0.01 = 50\,\text{m}^3/\text{day}$.

blocks.title: How long to reach a well?
blocks.q: A spill reaches the water table 200 m up-gradient of a well. $K = 5\,\text{m/day}$, $i = 0.005$, porosity $0.25$. How long until it arrives?
steps: Speed: $v = \dfrac{5 \times 0.005}{0.25} = 0.1\,\text{m/day}$.
Time: $200 \div 0.1 = 2,000$ days, about 5.5 years.

blocks.html: It is natural to imagine groundwater flowing in underground rivers as fast as a stream. Except in limestone caves, it creeps through tiny pores, often less than a meter a day. Check with the numbers: that is why a pollutant can take years to reach a well, and years more to flush out.

blocks.html: A glacier is a river of ice that flows downhill under its own weight. In Landforms Made by Water, Wind and Ice you saw what glaciers carve. Here we look at the glacier's budget, its income and its spending, and how that decides whether its end advances or retreats.

High on a glacier, more snow falls each winter than melts each summer: this is the accumulation zone. Low on it, melting wins: the ablation zone. The year's mass balance is gains minus losses. Meanwhile, gravity makes the ice flow downhill all the time, carrying ice from the accumulation zone to the ablation zone. The end of the glacier (the terminus) stays where ice arrives as fast as it melts. If melting wins, the terminus retreats, even though the ice keeps flowing forward, like walking forward on a moving walkway that runs backward faster than you walk.

A glacier gains snow up high and loses ice down low; its net mass balance is gains minus losses. The ice always flows downhill; the terminus advances or retreats depending on whether ice arrives faster than it melts.

blocks.name: es-landscape
blocks.cap: A mountain glacier with its accumulation and ablation zones. Change the mass balance and watch the terminus, while the ice keeps flowing downhill.

blocks.title: A year's balance
blocks.q: A glacier gains the equivalent of 1.5 m of water over its surface and loses 2.3 m. What is its net balance?
steps: Negative: the glacier lost mass. Most mountain glaciers worldwide have had negative balances for decades.

blocks.title: Moving the terminus
blocks.q: At its end, a glacier's ice flows forward 40 m a year, while melting removes 55 m of length a year. What happens to the terminus?
steps: $40 - 55 = -15\,\text{m}$ per year.
It retreats 15 m a year, while the ice itself still moves forward 40 m a year.

blocks.html: It is natural to think a retreating glacier is flowing backward, uphill. It isn't: the ice always flows downhill. Its end retreats because it melts faster than new ice arrives. Check with stakes drilled into the ice: they keep moving down-glacier even as the terminus pulls back.

Almost every rock contains a little copper, zinc or gold, spread thin among its other atoms. An ore is rock where geology has concentrated a metal enough to mine at a profit. In Renewable and Nonrenewable Resources you met minerals as resources; here we ask how nature gathers them, using the processes of weathering, magma, hot water and flowing streams.

head: Process
How it concentrates metal
Examples
rows: dense crystals settle and pile up as a magma cools
chromite layers; nickel and platinum ores
hot, salty water dissolves metals and deposits them in cracks as it cools
gold–quartz veins; porphyry copper around granite
rain carries away soluble elements and leaves insoluble ones behind
water dries up and leaves dissolved salts
running water sorts heavy grains from lighter sand
gold and tin in stream gravels
blocks.cap: Main ways ore deposits form.

blocks.html: What makes a deposit worth mining is its concentration factor, the ore grade divided by the metal's average abundance in the crust. Average continental crust holds only about 60 parts per million (ppm) of copper; typical copper ore is around 0.5% (5,000 ppm) or more, roughly 100 times richer. Rare metals need far larger factors: gold averages a few parts per billion, so gold ore of a few grams per tonne is concentrated about a thousand times. Each process above is a natural sorting machine that achieves this.

Ores are rare places where geology concentrated a metal far above its crustal average, by magma, hot water, weathering, evaporation or running water. Concentration factor = ore grade ÷ crustal abundance.

blocks.title: How concentrated?
blocks.q: Average crust holds about 60 ppm of copper. A mine works ore that is 0.6% copper. What is the concentration factor?

blocks.title: Metal from ore
blocks.q: A mine processes 50,000 tonnes of 0.5% copper ore. How much copper does it yield, if all is recovered?
steps: $50,000 \times 0.005 = 250\,\text{t}$ of copper.
The other 49,750 t become waste rock (tailings), which is why mines leave such large piles behind.

blocks.html: It is natural to think a metal can be mined wherever it occurs. In ordinary rock it is far too dilute: getting copper out of average crust would cost far more energy and money than the copper is worth. Check the concentration factor: ore needs about 100 times the crustal average for copper, and much more for rare metals like gold.

blocks.html: Coal, oil and natural gas are nonrenewable resources: they store energy captured from sunlight by living things millions of years ago. Where and how they form follows from depositional environments and the geothermal gradient.

Most oil and gas began as microscopic algae and plankton that settled into seafloor mud where oxygen was low, so they did not fully rot. Buried kilometers deep, the organic-rich mud (now shale, the source rock) warms along the geothermal gradient. Between about $60$ and $120^\circ\text{C}$ (the oil window) the organic matter breaks down into oil; hotter, it cracks into natural gas. Oil and gas are lighter than water, so they seep upward through the rock until something stops them. An oil field needs a porous, permeable reservoir rock (sandstone or limestone), an impermeable seal above it (shale or salt), and a trap that gathers the oil, such as the crest of an anticline. Coal has a different origin: plants in swamps, buried as peat and turned by heat and pressure into lignite, bituminous coal and anthracite.
Oil and gas form from buried plankton and algae cooked at about 60 to 120 °C, then migrate up into porous reservoir rock and collect under a seal in a trap. Coal forms from buried swamp plants.

blocks.name: es-structures
blocks.cap: An anticline: oil rising through a porous layer collects at the crest, under a sealing layer, a classic trap.

blocks.title: Depth of the oil window
blocks.q: In a basin, the surface is $15^\circ\text{C}$ and the gradient is $30^\circ\text{C/km}$. Between what depths does the oil window lie?
steps: Bottom ($120^\circ\text{C}$): $(120 - 15) \div 30 = 3.5\,\text{km}$.

blocks.title: Name the parts
blocks.q: In an oil field, oil fills the pores of a sandstone under a layer of salt, at the top of a dome-shaped fold. Name the reservoir, seal and trap.
steps: Reservoir: the porous sandstone that holds the oil.
Seal: the salt, which oil cannot pass through.
Trap: the dome (an anticline in every direction), which gathers the oil at its top.
blocks.a: Sandstone reservoir, salt seal, dome trap.

blocks.html: A popular idea is that oil comes from dinosaurs. Most oil formed from tiny algae and plankton buried in seafloor mud; there were never nearly enough dinosaurs to make it, and many oil fields are far older or younger than the dinosaurs. Check the source rocks: they are fine-grained marine shales rich in microscopic organic matter.

How long will a mineral or fuel last? Answering that needs two careful definitions, because ore deposits and fossil fuels are counted in different ways depending on what is known and what is profitable.

items: Resources: all of a material that exists in a form that could someday be extracted, including deposits not yet found or too poor or costly to use today.
Reserves: the part of the identified resources that can be produced at a profit now, with today's prices and technology.

blocks.html: Because reserves depend on economics, they change. Higher prices or better technology turn lower-grade resources into reserves; new discoveries add more; lower prices shrink them. A common yardstick is the reserves-to-production ratio, R/P = reserves ÷ yearly production: how many years today's reserves would last at today's rate. It is a snapshot, not a countdown. For many materials, reserves have grown about as fast as they were used for decades. On the other hand, if use grows by a fraction $r$ each year, the reserves run down faster than R/P suggests: adding up the growing yearly use gives $n = \dfrac{\ln(1 + r\cdot R/P)}{\ln(1 + r)}$ years. Economists and geologists debate how these effects will balance for each resource, and the answers differ from material to material.

Reserves are the part of a resource that can be produced at a profit today. R/P shows how long reserves would last at today's rate, but reserves change with price, technology and discovery, and use can grow or shrink.

blocks.name: graph

blocks.title: R/P
blocks.q: A country has reserves of 800 million tonnes and produces 20 million tonnes a year. What is R/P?
steps: $800 \div 20 = 40$ years.
That does not mean the material runs out in 40 years: reserves will change as prices, technology and discoveries change.

blocks.title: With growing use
blocks.q: Reserves equal 50 years of today's production. If use grows 2% a year and no reserves are added, how long do they last?
steps: $n = \dfrac{\ln(1 + 0.02 \times 50)}{\ln 1.02} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{\ln 1.02} = \dfrac{0.693}{0.0198} \approx 35$ years.
Growth shortens the time; discoveries, recycling and substitutes lengthen it.

blocks.html: Reading "reserves ÷ yearly use = 40 years" as the date a resource runs out is a common misreading. Reserves grow and shrink with prices, technology and new discoveries, and use can rise or fall. Check the definition: reserves are only what is known and profitable today.
